en: The First *Bhāvanākrama* composed by Ācārya Kamalaśīla [which sets forth the rules of conduct for a beginner regarding the Mahāyāna sūtras].
With reference to that, the stages of meditation (bhāvanākrama) are now briefly described.
Those who wish to attain omniscience without delay should, in brief, exert themselves in three areas: compassion, the spirit of enlightenment, and correct practice.
Knowing that compassion alone is the root cause of all qualities of Buddhahood without exception, it should be cultivated from the very beginning.

As it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*: "Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Blessed One: 'Blessed One, a bodhisattva need not train in an excessive number of dharmas.'"
"Blessed One, there is one dharma that a bodhisattva should thoroughly master and fully penetrate;
for him, all the qualities of a Buddha will then be as if held in the palm of his hand. What is that one dharma?"
That is to say, great compassion.
Blessed One, through great compassion, all the qualities of a Buddha come to be held in the palm of the hands of bodhisattvas.
Just as, Blessed One, wherever the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch proceeds, there the entire military force follows.
In the same way, Blessed One, wherever the great compassion of a bodhisattva goes, there all the qualities of a Buddha go.
Just as, Blessed One, when the life-faculty exists, the other faculties function;
"In the same way, Blessed One, when great compassion exists, there is the arising of the other qualities of the bodhisattvas.
Thus it is said in the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśa*: "Furthermore, Reverend Śāradvatīputra..."
The great compassion of the bodhisattvas is also inexhaustible.
Why is that?
Because it is the precursor.
Just as,
Reverend Śāradvatīputra, inhalations and exhalations are the precursors to a person’s life-faculty, so it is.
"In the same way, for the bodhisattva’s attainment of the equipment for the Mahāyāna, great compassion is the precursor," and so forth.
And it is said in the *Ārya-gayāśīrṣa*: "Mañjuśrī, what is its starting point?"
"What is the conduct of bodhisattvas, and what is its basis?
Mañjuśrī replied, "It originates from great compassion."
“O son of the gods,
the conduct of bodhisattvas has sentient beings as its basis,” and so on in detail.

For it is by being impelled by that [compassion] that Bodhisattvas, regardless of their own selves and solely for the sake of benefiting others, engage in the labor of accumulating the provisions (*sambhāra*), even though it involves extreme hardship and extends over a long period of time.

Thus it is said in the *Ārya-śraddhābalādhāna*: "In that regard, through great compassion as well, for the sake of maturing all sentient beings, there is no source of happiness whatsoever that he does not relinquish."
Therefore, by engaging in what is exceedingly difficult to perform, one will, before long, fulfill the accumulations and necessarily attain the state of omniscience.
Thus, compassion alone is the root of the Buddha-qualities.

It is precisely because they are embraced by great compassion that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having attained the state of omniscience, remain performing miraculous deeds for the benefit of the entire world; this very [compassion] is what constitutes the Blessed Ones' non-abiding in nirvāṇa.
Great compassion is the cause.
It increases through the frequent practice of mental attention directed toward suffering sentient beings.

One should cultivate [this compassion] toward all sentient beings by reflecting that all those beings belonging to the three realms are indeed utterly afflicted with suffering, according to their respective application to the three types of suffering.
And likewise, those who are hell-beings have been described by the Blessed One as being submerged in rivers of various long-lasting sufferings such as burning;
similarly, the hungry ghosts (*preta*) also experience intense suffering, their bodies completely withered by the affliction of the fires of unbearable and fierce hunger, thirst, and so forth.
The Blessed One has described how [certain beings] do not obtain even for a hundred years the opportunity to consume impure matter or a lump of spittle, and so forth.
Even animals are clearly seen experiencing manifold sufferings through mutual devouring, anger, killing, violence, and the like.

For instance, some have their bodies rendered helpless by the piercing of their noses, beatings, and binding; being tormented on all sides, they are exhausted in body by the burden of carrying extremely heavy loads against their will, however much they may resist.
Likewise, even those living in the forest who are innocent are sometimes sought out and killed for some purpose;
and with minds perpetually agitated by fear, they remain fleeing here and there—their immeasurable suffering is indeed visible.
Similarly, even in the human state, the suffering of hell is clearly seen.

In this regard, those such as thieves who are subjected to the cutting off of limbs, impalement on stakes, hanging, and so forth, experience suffering exactly like that of the denizens of hell. Those who are afflicted by poverty and the like experience suffering through hunger, thirst, and so on, just like the hungry ghosts (*preta*s).
And those such as servants whose very selves have been made dependent upon others—
And those who, being overcome by the powerful, are oppressed— such as through beating, confinement, and so forth, like animals—
they experience immeasurable suffering caused by the pursuit [of wealth], by mutual injury and harm, and by separation from the beloved and union with the unpleasant.
Even those who are in some places lords and appear to be happy, their prosperity is destined for ruin, and they are submerged in the thicket of various wrong views.

Accumulating various afflictions and karmas that cause the experience of the sufferings of the hells and other realms, beings dwelling in the causes of suffering—like trees on the edge of a precipice—are in truth truly suffering.

As for the gods, even those belonging to the desire realm have minds ignited by the fierce fire of sensual desire; their minds are as if distracted and their hearts are turbid, so that they do not attain mental composure for even a single moment.

For those who are impoverished of the wealth of the happiness of tranquility, what indeed can that happiness be called? How can those who are struck by the fear and sorrow of constant falling and degradation be said to be happy?
And as for those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, they too—

Even if they have for some time transcended the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), nevertheless, because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have not been utterly abandoned, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) still exists for them, since there is the possibility of falling again into the miserable states such as the hells. Indeed, all gods and humans are truly afflicted by the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), due to their dependence on afflictions, karma, and so forth.

Thus, having understood that the entire world is indeed consumed by the flames of the fire of suffering, and reflecting that "just as suffering is unpleasant to me, so too is it unpleasant to others," one should cultivate compassion toward all sentient beings.
First of all, it should be cultivated toward those on the side of friends, observing them as they undergo the various sufferings previously described.

Then, by means of the equality of sentient beings, one who perceives no distinction and reflects that in beginningless saṃsāra there is not a single being who has not been one's relative hundreds of times should cultivate [compassion] toward neutral persons.

When compassion arises equally toward neutral persons as toward those on the side of friends, then it should likewise be cultivated toward the side of enemies through mental attention to the equality of sentient beings and so forth.
And when it functions with equal intensity even toward the side of enemies as toward the side of friends, then one should gradually cultivate it toward all sentient beings in the ten directions.

And when compassion— which has the form of the desire to remove suffering— arises spontaneously and functions equally toward all sentient beings, just as it does toward those dear ones who are suffering, [then it has been perfected].
At that time, it becomes perfected and receives the designation of "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*),
as described in the *Akṣayamati-sūtra*. Furthermore,
this sequence for the cultivation of compassion was taught by the Blessed One in the *Abhidharma-sūtra* and other texts.

Through the power of such practice of compassion and by means of the vow to deliver all sentient beings, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) arises effortlessly in the form of a prayer for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

As it is said in the *Āryadaśadharmasūtra*: "Having seen sentient beings who are without protection, without refuge, and without an island, one establishes the mind in compassion and generates the thought of awakening up to [the attainment of] unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."

Even if a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) arises through the exhortation of others and so forth, nevertheless, that thought of awakening which arises in the bodhisattva spontaneously through the force of compassion has been described by the Blessed One as being more distinguished in the *Āryatathāgatajñānamudrāsamādhi*.
Thus, this very *bodhicitta*, even if devoid of practice, has been described by the Blessed One as having great fruit within *saṃsāra*.
And so it is said in the *Maitreyavimokṣa*: "In this way, noble son,..."
Even when broken, a diamond jewel surpasses all exceptionally fine gold ornaments;
it does not lose its name as a "diamond jewel," and it dispels all poverty.
In the same way, noble son,
even when its practice is impaired, the diamond-jewel of the resolve for omniscience surpasses all the golden ornaments of the qualities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
it does not lose the name "bodhicitta."
"And it turns back the poverty of cyclic existence.
Even one who is entirely incapable of training in the perfections in every way and by every means must nevertheless certainly generate the spirit of enlightenment.
Because it yields great fruit through being embraced by skillful means,
as it is said in the *Āryarājāvavādaka-sūtra*: "Since you, Great King,
have many duties and much that must be done..."
It is impossible for you to train in every way in all the perfections, from the perfection of generosity up to the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, O Great King, you should likewise cultivate desire, faith, aspiration, and resolve for perfect enlightenment.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, eating, or drinking,
constantly and continuously remember, attend to, and cultivate [it].
Having gathered together the roots of merit of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary persons, as well as your own, belonging to the past, future, and present,
rejoice with the supreme rejoicing. Having rejoiced,
offer these as acts of worship to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.
Having offered them, make them common to all sentient beings;

then, for the sake of all sentient beings until they attain omniscience and for the sake of fulfilling all the qualities of a Buddha, dedicate them three times each day toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this very way, O Great King, practicing thus, you shall exercise your sovereignty.
"And you shall not neglect the duties of kingship,
[and you shall fulfill the accumulations for awakening]," and having said this and more, he said: "Furthermore, O Great King..."
"By the ripening of the roots of merit from the thought of perfect enlightenment, you have been reborn among the gods many times;
you have been reborn among human beings many times;
and in all those births among gods and humans, you shall exercise sovereign authority."
Thus it is said in detail.
Furthermore, it is established that the bodhicitta which has practice as its essence yields an exceedingly vast fruit.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Āryavīradattaparipṛcchā*:
If the merit arising from the thought of awakening were to take on a physical form,
it would completely fill the realm of space and exceed it even further.
If a person were to give to the Lords of the World Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filled entirely with jewels;
“And whoever, with palms joined, inclines his mind toward awakening—this worship excels [all others], for its end is not found.
Thus it is described in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*: “O noble son, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)...”
"It is the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha," and so forth.
And that bodhicitta is twofold: the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhicitta*) and the mind of application (*prasthānacitta*). This is described in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*.
Likewise: "O son of good family, those beings in the world of beings who set their aspiration upon unexcelled perfect enlightenment are rare."
"Even rarer than those are the beings who have set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The volition that first takes the form of a prayer, "May I become a Buddha for the sake of the welfare of the entire world," is the *praṇidhicitta* (the mind of aspiration).
From the moment they are seen engaging in the accumulations while abiding in the undertaking of the vows, that is the "mind of setting out" (*prasthānacitta*).
Furthermore, the vow should be received from another—a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who is knowledgeable and capable of abiding in the vows.
In the absence of a suitable recipient [of the vow], one should generate the mind of awakening by bringing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas to mind, just as Mañjuśrī did when he was King Ambarāja.
Having thus generated the thought of awakening, the bodhisattva himself gives gifts and so forth and applies himself to practice, thinking: "One who is not himself tamed cannot tame others.
Furthermore, awakening is not attained without practice.
As it is said in the *Āryagayāśīrṣa*: "Awakening belongs to those bodhisattvas for whom practice is essential, not to those for whom practice is not essential.
And it is said in the *Āryasamādhirāja*: "Therefore, O Prince, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall become one for whom practice is essential.'"
For what reason? Because,
young man, for one whose essence is practice, it is so.
“Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain.

Furthermore, that practice of the bodhisattva—divided into the perfections (*pāramitā*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the bases of sympathy (*saṅgrahavastu*), and so forth—is described in detail in sūtras such as the *Akṣayamati* and the *Ratnamegha*.
Likewise, a bodhisattva must train even in the fields of worldly arts and crafts.
How much more so, then, regarding supramundane meditations and the like?
Otherwise, how could they accomplish the welfare of sentient beings in all its aspects?
And this practice of the bodhisattva, in brief, consists of wisdom and skillful means; it is neither wisdom alone nor skillful means alone.
As it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "Skillful means devoid of wisdom, and wisdom devoid of skillful means, are a bondage for bodhisattvas.
Wisdom accompanied by skillful means and skillful means accompanied by wisdom are described as liberation.
And it is also said in the *Āryagayāśīrṣa*: "These two are the concise paths of the bodhisattvas."
Endowed with two paths, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. What are these two?

"Skillful means (*upāya*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). In this context, setting aside the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), everything else— namely, the perfections such as generosity (*dāna*), the articles of attraction (*saṅgrahavastu*), and so forth, which comprise all wholesome qualities that gather together all forms of worldly excellence, including the purification of the field, great wealth, an abundant retinue, the ripening of sentient beings, emanations, and the like— is called "skillful means."
Wisdom (*prajñā*), however, is the cause for discerning the non-perverted nature of that very same skillful means (*upāya*).

For by means of it, having correctly distinguished the skillful means, one who is free from error does not become defiled while performing the welfare of oneself and others as they truly are—just as one who consumes poison held under the protection of a mantra is not harmed.
And thus it is said in this very sūtra: "Skillful means is the knowledge of gathering; wisdom is the knowledge of discernment."
Thus it is said.
And in the *Ārya-śraddhābalādhāna*, it is stated: "What is skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*)?
It is the gathering together of all phenomena."
"What is wisdom? It is skill regarding all phenomena through their non-differentiation.
Both of these—wisdom and means—must be cultivated at all times even by those who have entered the stages, and not wisdom alone nor means alone.

For it is taught that in all ten stages (*bhūmi*), beginning with the *Dṛḍhabhūmika* and others, the Bodhisattva practices the perfections (*pāramitā*), because of the statement: "and he does not fail to practice them in the remaining [stages].
Furthermore, the exhortation by the Buddhas to rouse the Bodhisattva dwelling in tranquility on the eighth stage would be contradicted [if he were not practicing them];
and this [fact] is to be understood from its mention there.
[And as it is said in that very sūtra: “Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror,

when a bodhisattva has thus entered this immovable bodhisattva stage and abides sustained by the power of his previous vows, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, effect the bestowal of the Tathāgata’s wisdom within that stream of the entrance to the Dharma.”
And they speak to him thus: "Excellent, excellent, noble son!
This is the ultimate patience for the sake of following the Buddha-dharmas."
Moreover, noble son, that perfection of the Buddha-qualities consisting of the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses which we possess does not belong to you.
Exert yourself in the pursuit of that abundance of the Buddha-qualities;
arouse your vigor!
Do not abandon this very gateway of patience.
Moreover, noble son,
although you have indeed attained this dwelling in peaceful liberation,

you should nevertheless take into account and look with compassion upon these foolish commoners who are not at peace nor tranquil, who are beset by the manifestation of various afflictions, and whose minds are afflicted by diverse discursive thoughts.
Moreover, noble son,
remember your former vow to bring about the welfare of sentient beings and the inconceivability of the gateways of gnosis.
Furthermore, noble son, [remember this].
This is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena:

whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this true nature remains fixed, the stability of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), which is to say, the emptiness of all phenomena and the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
It is not by this alone that the Tathāgatas are distinguished.
For even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas attain this very non-conceptual nature of phenomena (*avikalpadharmatā*).

Nevertheless, noble son, look now at our immeasurable bodies, our immeasurable knowledge, our immeasurable buddha-fields, our immeasurable accomplishment of knowledge, and our immeasurable circles of light.
and the immeasurability of the purity of the components of the voice;
in that very same way, you too should bring forth such accomplishment.
Furthermore, noble son, [you should do so].
But this is the one light, which is the light of non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena. Furthermore, noble son,
such lights of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas are infinite in their reach, infinite in their accomplishment, and infinite in their application.
For whom there is no number, no calculation, no measure, no proximate cause, and no analogy;
Exert yourself to bring about the realization of these;
furthermore, noble son,
look now upon the immeasurable nature of the fields in the ten directions, the immeasurable nature of sentient beings, and the immeasurable differentiation of dharmas.
Calculate all of that;
produce its realization exactly as it is.
"For thus, O Son of the Conqueror,"
Those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
provide for the bodhisattva who has thus entered the stages such immeasurable and incalculable gateways for the accomplishment of gnosis as these;
by means of those gateways for the accomplishment of gnosis, the bodhisattva brings to completion the activity of accomplishment through the differentiation of immeasurable gnosis.
"I announce to you, O Son of the Conqueror,

I declare to you: if those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were not to introduce that Bodhisattva into these gateways for the accomplishment of the knowledge of omniscience, then that itself would be his final nirvana, and the work for the sake of all sentient beings would come to rest."
Thus it is said in detail.
Furthermore, what is stated in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa* and in the *Gayāśīrṣa* also contradicts what was previously stated,
because there it is expressed in such a general manner.
Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Sarvadharmasaṅgrahavaipulya* would also be contradicted;
for it is said therein: "Subtle indeed, Mañjuśrī, is [this matter]..."
The karmic obstruction of rejecting the true Dharma:
Mañjuśrī, whoever conceives of one teaching spoken by the Tathāgata as being excellent, [while deprecating another].
"One conceives the notion of impurity toward a single [verse];
he thus rejects the true Dharma.
By rejecting the true Dharma, he slanders the Tathāgata. Having spoken at length in this way, he said: "Maitreya, as for this person..."
The complete realization of the six perfections is for the enlightenment of bodhisattvas; yet those deluded persons will speak thus:
"A bodhisattva should train only in the perfection of wisdom;
what is the use of the remaining perfections?"
They consider the other perfections, such as skillful means, to be something that should be disparaged.
What do you think, Ajita?
Was that King of Kāśi unwise, who gave his own flesh to the hawk for the sake of the dove?
Maitreya said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Maitreya, those which have been taught by me..."
"While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, roots of merit associated with the six perfections were accumulated.
Was any harm done by those roots of merit?
Maitreya replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said,
"Ajita, you yourself have for sixty eons fully accomplished the perfection of giving."
"Up until he has fully realized the perfection of wisdom for sixty eons,
those deluded men will say to him: 'Awakening is by means of a single method alone, namely, the method of emptiness,'" and so forth.

And it is said in the *Vairocanābhisambodhi*: "This very wisdom of omniscience has compassion as its root, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) as its cause, and skillful means (*upāya*) as its culmination.
Therefore, both must be cultivated by the bodhisattva at all times;
for in this way, the non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) of the Blessed Ones is accomplished.

For thus, because the Blessed Ones embrace the perfection of the fruits of skillful means such as generosity—namely, the excellence of a physical body, a field, a retinue, and great wealth—they do not abide in nirvana.
And because they have abandoned all cognitive distortions through wisdom, they do not abide in samsara, since samsara has its root in cognitive distortion.
Furthermore, by means of the practice consisting of the nature of wisdom and skillful means, the Middle Way is revealed through the avoidance of the extremes of superimposition and denial.

Because one avoids the extreme of superimposition through wisdom and avoids the extreme of denial through skillful means, it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti*: “One takes delight in the perfection of the form-body with its primary and secondary marks,
yet does not take delight merely in the realization of the dharma-body.”
It has been stated again: “The manifestation of the Tathāgatas, produced through wisdom and skillful means, is to be understood as arising from dependence upon others.
Furthermore, it has been stated: “By those who understand the discourse on the Dharma to be like a raft, even dharmas themselves must be abandoned, let alone non-dharmas.”

This was stated with the intention that [the teachings] are to be abandoned by means of relinquishing attachment to their opposites; however, it does not mean that they should not be relied upon even for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose.
Thus it has been said: "The Dharma is to be grasped, but not clung to."
The meaning is that [the mind] must be restrained by means other than the wrong path.

Furthermore, as for the fact that generosity and so forth are sometimes described as having worldly results, this was previously stated with reference to those who lack wisdom; it is intended to encourage those who are satisfied with merely that much root of virtue toward the higher roots of virtue.
Otherwise, the entire *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa* and other previously mentioned texts would be contradicted.
Therefore, it is established that both wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) must be cultivated.
In this regard, generosity and the other perfections receive the designation of "pāramitās" only when embraced by wisdom, and not otherwise.
Therefore, having established meditative concentration for the sake of purifying generosity and the rest, one should exert effort in order to acquire wisdom.
In that process, first of all, the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) must be generated.
For first, by means of that [scriptural wisdom], one determines the meaning of the scriptures;
then, by means of the wisdom consisting of reflection, one penetrates the definitive meaning as distinguished from the interpretable meaning;
thereafter, having ascertained the true meaning by means of that [wisdom], one should cultivate it, not what is unreal.
For otherwise, because even that which is erroneous would be cultivated and because doubt would not be eliminated, the arising of right knowledge would not occur;
consequently, cultivation would be as futile as that of the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika).

And it was said by the Blessed One in the *Samādhirāja*: "If one examines the phenomena as being without self, and having examined them, if one meditates upon them—that is the cause for attaining the fruit of nirvāṇa; any other cause does not lead to peace."
Therefore, having investigated with the wisdom born of reflection through both reasoning and scripture, one should cultivate the very nature of reality as it truly is.
And the nature of things, when determined through both scripture and reasoning from the perspective of ultimate truth, is indeed non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Regarding this, according to scripture, it is said in the *Ārya-dharmasaṅgīti*: "Non-arising is the truth; all other phenomena are not the truth."
And this is called "non-arising is the truth" because it accords with the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);
however, from the perspective of the ultimate reality itself, there is neither arising nor non-arising, because that [ultimate reality] transcends all conventional designations (*vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place: "O son of good family, the world's abode is intent upon arising and cessation;
therefore, the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, has spoken by way of conventional usage in order to avoid being a cause of terror for the world."
"It arises and ceases, yet herein there is no arising of any dharma whatsoever.
And it is said in the *Āryabuddhasaṃgīti*: "What is the fundamental inquiry? What is the fundamental [nature]?"
He said: "Non-arising is the source;
inquiry into that is 'thorough inquiry' (*yoniśaḥ pṛcchā*).
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place: "All phenomena have the letter *ca* as their gateway; they are free from death and rebirth."
"All phenomena have non-existence as their gateway,
by virtue of the emptiness of intrinsic nature. And in the *Āryasatyadvayavibhāga*, it is stated that through the equality of non-arising, there is the equality of all phenomena.
And it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: “Subhūti, form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form,
up to consciousness, which is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness— this being based on the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaśūnyatā*).”
And it is said in the *Hastikakṣya*:
"No entity whatsoever is found for which there is the possibility of arising;
regarding phenomena that are impossible [to arise], the fool desires their possibility."
And it is said in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*: “All these phenomena are all equal through the equality of the three times;
in the past time, all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, and so on, up to the present time. Thus, first of all, one should investigate by means of scripture (*āgama*).
For when the meaning of the scriptures has been stabilized through reasoning, it cannot be refuted by others;
therefore, one should also investigate it through reasoning.
In this regard, reasoning is stated in brief:
The arising of entities must be either without cause or with a cause.
First, it cannot be without cause, because we observe that they occur only occasionally.
For if they were independent of causes, then—since there would be no distinguishing factor—they would not exist only at the time of their production, but rather would exist always and everywhere.
Or, because there would be no distinction from the time of non-existence, they would not exist even at the time of production;
thus, first of all, it is not logical for them to be without a cause, nor is it logical for them to have a cause.
For instance, those entities do not arise from a permanent cause such as Īśvara or others imagined by the non-Buddhists, because they are observed to arise sequentially.
It is not logical for a result whose causes are complete to arise sequentially, since it would be independent [of conditions].
Nor can there be dependence on another for Īśvara or others who are themselves inherently capable.
Because that which is eternal cannot be assisted by others, and because dependence is impossible for that which provides no assistance;
for this very reason, since Īśvara and the like are devoid of all causal capacity, they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) just like the son of a barren woman and so forth.
Because a real entity is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*),
it has been demonstrated through analysis that these [entities] lack the capacity for any effect either successively or simultaneously.

For instance, if every effect has been produced once, and that [cause] remains capable of production even at a subsequent time, then—provided its capable nature persists—there follows the undesirable consequence of the effect being produced again as before;
or, if that nature does not persist, there follows the undesirable consequence of impermanence due to the abandonment of its prior nature. Therefore, no such thing as a permanent entity exists.

Therefore, it was said by the Blessed One: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, the superimposition of the non-existent is the superimposition of an attachment to unconditioned entities such as space, cessation, and nirvāṇa.
Consequently, their arising from an eternal cause is not logical.

Nor can it arise from the impermanent; for since the past and the future lack substantial reality, it is not logical for [the effect] to be produced from them, as that would entail the consequence of being causeless.
Nor can it arise from the present, because production from it is impossible whether [the cause and effect] are simultaneous or non-simultaneous.
For instance, a cause cannot be simultaneous [with its effect], because the effect, like the cause's own nature, is already established by virtue of existing at that same time.
Nor can it be at a different time, because if production occurred after an interval of another time, it would follow that the effect arises from what is already past and so forth.

Even if [the effect] were to arise without an interval, if that non-interval were by way of its entire self, then because all moments would enter into a single moment, it would follow that an eon (*kalpa*) would be nothing more than a single moment.
This is just as, for example, if an atom were to unite with another by way of its entire self, it would follow that a mass would be no larger than a single atom.
Alternatively, [if the non-interval were] by way of a single part...
In that case, it would follow that a moment possesses parts.
Nor do they arise from themselves, because this position is already subsumed under the thesis of causelessness, and because there is a contradiction in an action operating upon itself.
Nor can they exist in both ways, because that would entail the inclusion of the two faults inherent in each respective position.
Therefore, in the ultimate sense, these entities are simply unarisen.
However, because arising exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*), there is no contradiction with scripture and other authorities.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"Entities exist conventionally; in the ultimate sense (*paramārthe*), they are not entities."
"The error regarding things that lack intrinsic nature— that is conventional truth.
This reasoning is intended by the Blessed One in the *Śālistamba* and other works,
because he refutes arising from self, from another, from both, and without a cause.
Alternatively, one should investigate by means of reasoning as follows:
entities are of two kinds, those with form and those without form.
Among these, first, material things such as jars do not possess a single intrinsic nature, because they are divided into atoms whose forms are distinct.

Even if it is not established that atoms situated in a preceding and succeeding position are divided into directional parts such as the east and so forth, it is nonetheless illogical for them to possess a manifold nature if they consist of an accumulation of atoms;

nor is there any other ontological nature apart from a unitary or manifold nature. Thus, these material entities are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), like the forms perceived in dreams and the like.
And this was stated by the Blessed One himself in the *Ārya-Laṅkāvatāra*: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the horns of a cow..."
"Even when divided down to the atom, it does not remain;
furthermore, even atoms, when divided, do not remain as characterized by the nature of an atom.
And those things which are formless, when analyzed in the same way, are likewise devoid of intrinsic nature.

For indeed, since external objects such as blue and so forth do not exist, one must accept that by their very nature the formless aggregates, beginning with consciousness, manifest in the form of blue and so on.
And it was said by the Blessed One: "There is no external form; it is one's own mind that appears externally."

Furthermore, because they manifest with variegated forms such as blue and so forth, and because they manifest with the forms of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, it is not logical for these to possess a single intrinsic nature (*ekasvabhāva*).
Nor is it logically tenable for a single entity to have multiple forms,
due to the contradiction between the one and the many.
If a certain single intrinsic nature is not established, then multiplicity is also illogical,
because the manifold consists of a collection of unities.
Alternatively, one might accept that these forms such as color and so forth appear there as mere unrealities.
In that case, consciousness also becomes unreal,
because it is not distinct from its own nature;
for there is no other nature of consciousness apart from its self-luminous character.
Furthermore, forms and other objects do not manifest by themselves;
and since they are unreal once they have assumed the nature of consciousness, it would follow that all consciousness is admitted to be unreal.
Therefore, the Blessed One stated: "Consciousness is like an illusion."
Therefore, it is certain that all these entities are ultimately unreal because they are empty of a nature that is either one or many.
And this point was stated by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra*:
"Just as a form in a mirror is devoid of being either identical to or different [from the object],"
"It is seen, yet it does not exist there; so it is with entities for you.
Regarding the phrase "devoid of oneness and otherness," the meaning is "free from oneness and otherness."
And it has been said again:
"When things are analyzed by the intellect, their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) cannot be apprehended;
therefore, they are shown to be inexpressible and devoid of intrinsic nature."

Having thus determined the true reality through the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*), one should generate the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*) in order to directly perceive that object.
It has been taught in such texts as the *Āryaratnamegha* that the object does not become directly perceived by means of mere extensive learning and the like;
furthermore, this is the experience of those who practice.
Furthermore, without the arising of the light of extremely clear knowledge, the darkness of the obscurations is not correctly abandoned;
and through the frequent practice of cultivation, extremely clear knowledge arises even regarding an unreal object.
Just as for those who have attained the meditative absorptions of the impure, the earth-kṛtsna, and so forth, [knowledge arises], how much more so in the case of the elements?
And thus, the fruitfulness of cultivation has been stated in the *Ārya-samādhirāja* by virtue of its result being clearly manifest knowledge:
"I announce and declare to you: in whatever way a person reflects extensively..."
In such and such a way, his mind becomes characterized by those thoughts, being dependent upon them.
Thus it is said in detail.
Therefore, one who desires to directly realize reality engages in meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
In that regard, first of all, the practitioner (*yogin*) must accomplish calm abiding (*śamatha*) in order to stabilize the mind.
Because the mind is as fickle as water, it has no stability without the support of calm abiding (*śamatha*);
and it is not possible to know things as they truly are with a mind that is not concentrated.
For it was said by the Blessed One: “One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are.

Calm abiding (śamatha) is accomplished more swiftly for one who is independent of desire for gain and the like, who is steadfast in right practice, whose nature is to endure suffering and other hardships, and who has initiated vigor.
For this very reason, in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana* and other scriptures, generosity and the other perfections are described in a progressive sequence.

Thus, established in the equipment for tranquility such as ethical discipline and so forth, having performed prostrations and other services toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in a location favorable to the mind, having carried out the confession of misdeeds and the rejoicing in merit, and having brought great compassion itself to the fore with the intention of uplifting the entire world, one should sit upon a comfortable seat with the body held straight, having assumed the cross-legged posture.
One should bring about the accomplishment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In that regard, first of all, one should fix the mind upon whatever object is to be investigated—in brief, by whatever means the entirety of objects is subsumed.
This is the concise [instruction]. (Bhk 182)
Furthermore, the object is twofold, distinguished as being with form (*rūpin*) and without form (*arūpin*).
For a beginner, it is appropriate first to take a concise object in order to avoid the fault of distraction.

However, when one has mastered mental attention (*manaskāra*), then, having purified it through the distinctions of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth, one may indeed take up the object in detail as well.
Likewise, in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other treatises, various kinds of objects of focus are taught for yogins according to the distinctions of the eighteen types of emptiness and so forth.

In this very context, out of compassion for sentient beings, the Blessed One has set forth the classification of entities in the *Abhidharma* and other works through concise, intermediate, and extensive expositions based on the distinctions of the form-possessing (*rūpin*) and formless (*arūpin*) categories.

Furthermore, one should enumerate those entities by way of their inclusion within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so on, in order to avoid the extremes of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*).
Then, having determined the entire collection of objects, one should again direct the mind toward that very [object] in a continuous stream.

However, if in the interim the mind should be distracted outwardly by passion or other such afflictions, one should recognize that state of distraction, pacify the distraction through the cultivation of the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth, and once more direct the mind toward that same object, higher and higher.
The sequence for the cultivation of the foul and so forth is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity.
But when one perceives that the mind is not delighted with that [object],
then one should cultivate delight therein by seeing the virtues of meditative concentration and should pacify lack of delight by seeing the faults of distraction.

Now, when the mind becomes sluggish due to being overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, such that the apprehension of the object is unclear, one should then pacify that sluggishness by cultivating the perception of the world or by reflecting on the qualities of the Buddha and other objects of joy; having done so, one should again grasp that very same object more firmly.

Then, when one perceives the mind becoming agitated in the interval while recollecting previous laughter, play, and so forth, one should pacify that agitation by reflecting on the spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) of impermanence and other such qualities;
thereafter, one should again exert effort to ensure that the mind flows toward that very same object without further volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Then, when one perceives that the mind is flowing naturally, having become even-paced through being free from both laxity and excitement, one should then practice equanimity by relaxing the effort of application.
However, if an effort of application is made while the mind is already even-paced, it will cause the mind to become distracted.
But when the mind proceeds toward that object, flowing without volitional effort for as long as desired, then it should be known that calm abiding (*śamatha*) has been accomplished.
And this is the general characteristic of all forms of calm abiding.
Because the nature of śamatha is merely one-pointedness of mind,
its object is indeed not fixed.
And this path of calm abiding was taught by the Blessed One in the Noble *Prajñāpāramitā* and other scriptures,
as it says: "Therein, one places the mind, one settles it thoroughly..."
He settles it, he establishes it, he tames it.
It calms it,
completely pacifies it,
and makes it one-pointed.
"He concentrates" [is explained] by means of nine terms. Therein, "he settles" means he binds [the mind] to the object of focus.
He establishes [the mind],
causing it to proceed continuously upon that very same object;
he settles it.
Having recognized that distraction, he avoids it;
he establishes [the mind], and having avoided distraction, he places it again and again upon that very same object.
It subdues [the mind] and generates delight;
it pacifies it and thoroughly calms discontent by seeing the faults of distraction;
it brings it to complete stillness.
One pacifies the emergence of sloth, torpor, and so forth;
one brings [the mind] to one-pointedness and exerts effort toward the state of flowing without volitional formation upon the object of focus.
He composes [the mind]; he maintains equanimity toward the mind that has attained equilibrium; this means he attends to it.
And this meaning of these terms has been explained by the former masters and by Maitreya.
In brief, there are six faults for every meditative concentration: laziness,
loss of the object of focus,
lethargy, and excitement.
Non-application and application:
as their antidotes, the eight formative forces of abandonment are to be cultivated.
Namely: faith, aspiration, exertion, and pliancy.
Mindfulness, clear comprehension, and volition.
And equanimity (*upekṣā*). Among these, the first four are the antidotes to laziness (*kausīdya*).
For it is thus: through faith (*śraddhā*), characterized by conviction in the qualities of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the practitioner’s aspiration for it arises.
From that aspiration, one should initiate vigor.
By the power of that vigor, one attains flexibility (*karmanya*) of body and mind.
Thereupon, for one whose body and mind are pliant, laziness (*kausīdya*) is turned away.
Therefore, faith and the other [faculties] should be cultivated for the sake of abandoning laziness.
Mindfulness is the antidote to the loss of the object of focus;
clear comprehension is the antidote to lethargy and excitement.
Because of that, one correctly discerns dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*).
However, at the time when dullness and agitation have not yet been pacified, the fault is non-application (*anābhoga*); as its antidote, volition (*cetanā*) should be cultivated.
When dullness and agitation have been pacified and the mind flows toward tranquility, then application (*ābhoga*) is the fault.
At that time, equanimity, which is the antidote to those [distractions], should be cultivated.

Endowed with these eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*) becomes supremely serviceable (*paramakarmaṇya*) and brings about qualities such as the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Therefore it is said in the Sūtra: “Endowed with the eight formative forces of abandonment, one cultivates the bases of psychic power.

And this one-pointedness of mind, through its association with progressively increasing flexibility (*karmaṇyatā*) and its connection with the specific qualities of the object and so forth, receives the designations of the dhyānas, the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so on.
For instance, when it is associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), it is thus.
Then it is called the "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*) because it is the mind of the preparatory stage for the first dhyāna.

And when it becomes secluded from sensual craving and unwholesome states, and is associated with applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and internal serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*), then it is called the first dhyāna.
For this very reason, the first dhyāna, when it is devoid of *vitarka* alone, is called the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
This occurs when it is free from both *vitarka* and *vicāra*, detached from craving for the level of the first dhyāna,
and associated with joy, bliss, and internal serenity (*adhyātmasamprasāda*).
Then it is called the second dhyāna;
however, when it becomes detached from craving for the level of the second dhyāna,
it becomes associated with pleasure, equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
Then it is called the third dhyāna;
when one becomes detached from craving for the level of the third dhyāna,
and there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure associated with equanimity and mindfulness.
Then, the fourth dhyāna is spoken of.

In this same way, it should be applied to the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and so forth, according to the distinctions of their objects (*ālambana*), aspects (*ākāra*), and other factors.
Thus, having stabilized the mind upon the object of focus, one should analyze it with wisdom;
for through the arising of the light of knowledge, the seed of delusion is utterly abandoned.
Otherwise, as is the case with the non-Buddhists, the afflictions would not be abandoned by mere meditative concentration alone.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Even if one should cultivate this samādhi, yet does not eliminate the notion of a self,
his afflictions will flare up again, just like Udraka’s cultivation of samādhi in this world."
In this regard, the sequence for the cultivation of wisdom is briefly set forth in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"Having ascended to mind-only, one should not conceptualize external objects;
abiding in the focal point of suchness, one should transcend even mind-only."
Having transcended mind-only, one should transcend the non-manifest;
the yogi established in the non-manifest beholds the Mahāyāna.
"Effortless movement is peaceful, purified by aspirations;
the supreme, selfless gnosis does not perceive anything in the non-manifest.
This is the meaning therein: first, the yogi should investigate those material phenomena which are imagined by others as being external objects.
Are these [objects] other than consciousness,
or is it rather that consciousness itself appears in such a way, as in the state of dreaming?
Therein, one should analyze [the object] externally, part by part, down to the level of atoms.

And as the yogi examines those atoms part by part, he does not perceive those external objects. As he does not perceive them, it occurs to him: "All this is merely mind; external objects do not exist. Thus it is:
“Having ascended to mind-only, one should not conceptualize external objects. This means that one should abandon the conceptual constructions of phenomena possessing form.
One should investigate those [objects] which have reached the conditions for perception by means of their non-perception.
Having thus analyzed material phenomena (*rūpin*), one should analyze immaterial phenomena (*arūpin*).

In that regard, even that which is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) is not tenable as a grasper when there is no graspable object, because a grasper depends upon a graspable object; therefore, the mind is devoid of both graspable and grasper—it is indeed non-dual mind.

“Abiding in the focal object of suchness, one should transcend even that ‘mind-only’; one should transcend the aspect of the grasper. The meaning is that one should abide in non-dual gnosis, which is the very absence of appearance of duality.”
In this way, having transcended mind-only, one should also transcend that non-dual cognition which is free from the appearance of duality.

One should reflect that since the arising of entities from themselves or from another is untenable, and since the apprehended object and the apprehending subject are unreal, it is likewise illogical for that [cognition] to possess reality, as it is not distinct from them.
Therein, one should abandon even the attachment to non-dual cognition as a real entity.
The meaning is that one should abide in a cognition that is non-dual knowledge and free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*).
This being so, one becomes established in the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena.
For one established therein, through the entry into the supreme reality, there occurs the entry into non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*).
And thus, when the yogin abides in that non-dual knowledge which is free from appearances, because he then abides in the supreme reality, he perceives the Mahāyāna.
This very perception of the supreme reality is what is called the Mahāyāna.

This alone is the vision of the supreme reality (*paramatattva*): for one who examines all phenomena with the eye of wisdom, there is the vision of truth through the illumination of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Thus it is said in the Sūtra: "What is the vision of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*)?
It is the non-seeing of all phenomena."

In this context, it is precisely this kind of non-perception that is intended, and not that non-perception which arises from a deficiency of cognition—as in the case of those with closed eyes or those born blind—or from a lack of mental attention (*amanasikāra*).

Consequently, because the latencies of the perversions, such as the adherence to existence (*bhāvābhiniveśa*), have not been abandoned, the multitude of afflictions beginning with attachment (*rāga*)—which is rooted in the adherence to existence—arises once again, just as it does for one who has emerged from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Thus, one is not liberated.
Thus should the yogi become.
Attachment and the other afflictions have been described in the *Āryasatyadvayanirdeśa* and other texts as being rooted in the adherence to the reality of phenomena (*bhāvābhiniveśa*).
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*: "By means of non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*), one abandons the signs (*nimitta*) of form and so forth."
In that regard as well, for one who investigates with wisdom, that which is non-apprehension is intended by "non-attention" (*amanasikāra*), and not merely the absence of attention.

For the attachment to form and so forth, which has existed since beginningless time—unlike the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the like—is not abandoned merely by the avoidance of attention.

Indeed, if doubt is not abandoned, it is impossible to avoid the mental engagement of attachment toward previously perceived forms and so forth, just as one cannot avoid being burned if one does not avoid fire.
In the same way, these false conceptual constructions regarding form and so forth should not be removed from the mind by hand as one would pluck out thorns;
rather, they are removed through the disappearance of the seed of doubt.

And that seed of doubt disappears for the yogi when, the light of meditative concentration being present, he examines with the eye of wisdom and finds the non-perception of those previously perceived forms and so forth, despite their having met the conditions for perception.
Just as the cognition of a snake [disappears] from a rope,
it departs and not otherwise;
likewise, through the removal of the seed of doubt, the mental attention toward signs such as form can be abandoned, and not otherwise.

Otherwise, if the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) were absent and there were no vision by means of the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*), then— just as for a person standing in a dark well who has doubt regarding the existence of jars and other objects located within it— the yogin’s doubt concerning the existence of forms and so forth would never cease. And because that doubt does not cease, the improper adherence to false forms and so forth would continue to arise, just as in one whose defect of cataracts has not been removed, and it could not be stopped by anything at all.

Therefore, having steadied the mind with the hand of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one should uproot the seed of false conceptualization regarding form and so forth from that consciousness by means of the weapon of extremely subtle wisdom (*prajñā*).
When this is done, false conceptualizations— like trees whose roots have been severed— will not sprout again in the mind, as they are rendered rootless.
For this very reason, the Blessed One has taught the path that proceeds by yoking together calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) for the sake of abandoning the obscurations,
because these two are the causes of non-conceptual correct knowledge (*avikalpa-samyagjñāna*).
And so it has been said:
"By being established in ethical discipline (śīla), one attains meditative concentration (samādhi); from the attainment of meditative concentration, there is the cultivation of wisdom (prajñā).
Through wisdom, knowledge becomes purified; for one whose knowledge is purified, there is the perfection of ethical discipline.
Thus, when the mind has been made stable upon an object through calm abiding (śamatha), then for one who investigates with wisdom, the light of right knowledge arises.
Then, as if illuminating darkness in the light, the obscuration is abandoned.

For this very reason, because these two—samādhi and wisdom—exist in mutual conformity toward the arising of right knowledge, like the eye and light, they do not stand in mutual opposition like light and darkness;
for samādhi does not have the nature of darkness.
Rather, it is characterized by one-pointedness of mind.

And because of the statement that "one who is concentrated understands things as they truly are," it is exclusively conducive to wisdom and not its opposite; therefore, for one who is concentrated and investigating with wisdom, there is the non-apprehension of all phenomena.
That itself is the supreme non-apprehension; and that state of the yogins, characterized by abiding, is effortless,
because beyond that there is nothing further to be seen.
It is "peaceful" (*śānta*) because of the subsiding of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) characterized by the discrimination of existence, non-existence, and so forth.
For instance, when a yogi, examining with wisdom, does not perceive any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity,
then no conceptualization of existence arises for him.
Even the conceptualization of non-existence does not exist for him at all;
for if existence were ever perceived,
then, by its negation, the conceptualization of non-existence would proceed.

But when an entity is not perceived by the yogin, even while examining it with the eye of wisdom throughout the three times, how could he then form a conceptual construction of non-existence through its negation?
In this way, other conceptual constructions as well do not arise for him at all, because of [the absence of] the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence. (Bhk 189)
Because all conceptual construction is pervaded [by this],
and because that which is pervaded cannot exist in the absence of the pervader;
this is that supreme non-conceptual yoga.

For the yogin established therein, because all conceptual constructions have subsided, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are completely abandoned.

For it has been described by the Blessed One in such works as the *Āryasatyadvayanirdeśa* that the root cause of the obscuration of afflictions is the inversion [of perceiving] existence and so forth regarding entities that are unarisen and unceasing.

And through this practice of yoga, because all conceptual constructions of existence and so forth are abandoned, there occurs the abandonment of the entire inversion of existence and so forth—which is of the nature of ignorance and is the root of the obscuration of afflictions.
Then, through the eradication of the root, the obscuration of the afflictions is completely abandoned.
Thus it is said in the *Satyadvayanirdeśa*: "Mañjuśrī, how do the afflictions go to their subdual?"
"How are the afflictions fully understood?
Mañjuśrī replied: "In ultimate reality, all phenomena are absolutely unborn, unarisen, and non-existent; yet, conventionally, there is the inversion of what is unreal.
From that inversion of the unreal arises conceptualization and discursive thought."
From that conceptualization and discursive thought arises improper mental attention;
from that improper mental attention arises the superimposition of a self;
and from that superimposition of a self arises the emergence of views.
From that obsession with views, the afflictions arise.
Furthermore, O Son of the Gods, he who understands all phenomena from the perspective of ultimate reality as being absolutely unborn, unarisen, and non-existent—
He is, in the ultimate sense, free from error;
and he who is free from error in the ultimate sense is non-conceptual;
and he who is non-conceptual is engaged in proper application.
And for one who is correctly applied to the practice, there is no superimposition of a self;
for one who has no superimposition of a self, there is no arising of views;
and so on, until ultimately, even the arising of all views, including the view of nirvāṇa, does not occur.
For one who thus dwells in non-arising, the afflictions should be seen as completely subdued;
this is called the subduing of the afflictions,
O Devaputra.

O Devaputra, when one understands through non-apparent gnosis that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the afflictions are absolutely empty, absolutely non-existent, and absolutely signless, then the afflictions are fully understood.
In this regard, O Devaputra, it is just as if someone who knows the lineage of a venomous snake were to pacify the poison of that venomous snake.
"In the same way, O Devaputra, the afflictions of one who understands the lineage (*gotra*) of the afflictions are pacified.
The Devaputra asked: "Which one, Mañjuśrī?"
It is the lineage (*gotra*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

He says: "To whatever extent there is this conceptual construction regarding all phenomena—which, from the perspective of ultimate reality, are absolutely unborn, unarisen, and non-existent—this is the lineage of the afflictions," and so forth.
Furthermore, because all forms of error are pervaded by the error [of grasping] at existence and so on.
Upon its abandonment, because all forms of error are abandoned, the obscuration to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is also correctly abandoned by him,
since obscuration is characterized by error.

And when the obscuration to the knowable is abandoned, due to the absence of any hindrance, the light of knowledge proceeds for the yogin as a direct perception, unimpeded everywhere— like the rays of the sun in a sky free from the obscurations of clouds and the like.
For consciousness has the nature of illuminating the intrinsic reality of an object;
and although that object is present, consciousness does not illuminate it because of the existence of an obstruction.
However, when the obstruction is absent, [it illuminates it].
Since he has attained a specific inconceivable power, why would he not manifest every single thing exactly as it is?
Therefore, through the thorough knowledge of all things exactly as they are, in both their conventional and ultimate forms, omniscience is attained.
Consequently, this alone is the supreme path for the abandonment of obscurations and the realization of omniscience.
However, because the path of the Śrāvakas and others does not eliminate [the root] misconceptions, the two obscurations are not correctly abandoned.
Thus it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: "But others, seeing all phenomena as dependent on causes, conceive the notion that there is nirvāṇa even within nirvāṇa.
Because they do not perceive the selflessness of phenomena, O Mahāmati, [true nirvāṇa] does not exist for them."
Mahāmati, liberation for those belonging to the lineage of the realization of the Śrāvaka-vehicle is the notion of having attained deliverance when there is actually no deliverance.
In this regard, Mahāmati—
"One should practice yoga for the turning away from false views.
For this very reason, because there is no liberation by any other path, the Blessed One has taught that there is only one vehicle (*ekayāna*).
It is solely with the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) of introducing the ignorant to the truth that the paths of the Śrāvakas and others were taught.
For in this way, by contemplating that "this is merely the aggregates and there is no self," the Śrāvaka enters into the selflessness of the person (pudgala-nairātmya);
and by contemplating that "the three realms are representation-only" (vijñaptimātra), the Vijñānavādin enters into the selflessness of external objects.
However, through this entry into selflessness by means of non-dual cognition, one enters into the supreme reality (*paramatattva*).
But the entry into mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātratā*) alone is not itself the entry into reality,
as was stated previously.
And it is said in the *Āryalokottaraparivarta*: "Furthermore, O Son of the Victor,
one enters into the triple world as mind-only,
and one enters into that mind as being without end or middle."
Because there is an absence of the middle characterized by duration between the two extremes characterized by arising and cessation, the mind is without end or middle.
Therefore, entry into non-dual gnosis itself is entry into reality.
From what is this state of the yogins purified? To this he says:
“Purified by vows”:
that which was vowed by the Bodhisattva through great compassion for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings—
by the power of that vow, and through the progressive cultivation of wholesome qualities such as giving and so forth, it has become thus purified.

By means of which, even while possessing the knowledge of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena, their regard for all sentient beings does not turn away; and as long as cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) lasts, they remain unstained by the defects of cyclic existence.
Furthermore, regarding how it is effortless and peaceful, he states the reason:
"One perceives with non-appearance the supreme, selfless knowledge."

Because even that non-dual knowledge characterized as non-duality— which is held by the proponents of non-duality to be the best and the ultimate truth— is seen by the yogi through a knowledge that is non-dual and free from appearances to be without self and devoid of intrinsic nature;
therefore, due to the absence of anything further to be seen, it is effortless (*anābhoga*).
Because of the absence of all conceptual constructions, it is "peaceful.
In this regard, who now exists as that yogi?
If it is argued that "he who sees [exists]," [we reply:
in ultimate reality, there is no independent self or the like,
nor does any yogi see anything.

However, conventionally, just as in the world it is consciousness itself that is designated in various ways—such as "Devadatta perceives Yajñadatta through cognition"—merely by virtue of the arising of a cognition bearing the aspect of objects such as form, and yet there is no self or anything else;
so too here, consciousness itself, arising as non-dual knowledge free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*), is designated in that way: "he perceives through non-apparent knowledge."

For even though all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is not the case that, conventionally (*saṃvṛti*), yogic cognition or other ordinary cognitions are not accepted.
Thus it is said in the *Āryasatyadvayanirdeśa*: "While there is absolute non-existence from the perspective of ultimate reality, one cultivates the path conventionally.
Otherwise, how could the distinctions between Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) be established?
However, that which lacks a cause even conventionally does not arise even conventionally,
such as a rabbit's horn and the like;
but that which possesses a cause certainly arises, even if it is ultimately unreal.
For example, like an illusion, a reflection, an echo, and so forth.

Nor does it follow that because illusions and the like arise dependently on the level of conventional reality, they must be real entities from the perspective of ultimate truth; for such things cannot withstand analytical investigation.
Therefore, the entire world is like an illusion.
Just as the illusion of the birth of sentient beings proceeds there through the power of the illusions of afflictions and karma,
so too does the illusion of the yogi’s knowledge proceed for yogis through the power of the illusions of the accumulations of merit and wisdom.
And so it is said in the Noble *Prajñāpāramitā*: "Some are emanations of Śrāvakas, some are emanations of Pratyekabuddhas, and some are emanations of Bodhisattvas."
Some are emanated by the Tathāgata,
some are emanated by the afflictions, and some are emanated by karma.
By this, Subhūti, [it is understood].
"In this way, all phenomena are produced as emanations.
However, this is the distinction of yogins from ordinary beings:
for, like a magician, because they thoroughly understand that illusion as it truly is, they do not adhere to it as being real. (Bhk 193)
Therefore, they are called "yogins.

Those who, like foolish ordinary beings (*bālapṛthagjana*), are attached to that [emptiness] as if it were a mere curiosity, are called "fools" because of their perverted attachment; thus, everything is consistent.
And so it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṅgīti*:
Just as a certain magician, intent on the liberation of a magical creation, has no attachment toward that creation because he has known it from the very beginning; so too is the case for the Buddha.

"Having realized that the three worlds are like a magical creation, one who has reached the further shore of perfect enlightenment girds himself for the sake of the world, even though he has already known the world to be thus. In this manner, one should meditate upon reality through this sequence.

And therein, one should pacify laxity, excitement, and so forth as they arise, just as before. However, when knowledge proceeds without effort upon the object of the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena, free from laxity, excitement, and the like,
then the path that carries the union of calm abiding and special insight has been perfected.
In this manner, as long as one is able, one should meditate while remaining on the stage of conduct through aspiration (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) by the power of aspiration.
Then, having risen from that state after assuming the cross-legged posture as desired, one should reflect again in this way:

"Even though these phenomena are indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they nonetheless remain established according to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*)."
And so it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*: "How does a bodhisattva become skilled in selflessness?
Here, noble son, a bodhisattva examines form with correct wisdom."
He examines feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Examining form, he does not perceive the arising of form,
nor does he perceive its cessation.
One does not apprehend its origination;
likewise, one does not apprehend the arising of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does one apprehend their cessation.
"One does not perceive an origination;
and this is from the perspective of ultimate reality for the wisdom that abides in non-arising, and not by way of a conventional nature," so it is said at length.
And these [beings] with the intellects of fools [perceive] things in this way, even though they are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Due to their adherence to perverted views, they wander in saṃsāra and experience various sufferings.

Bringing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) directly before him, he should reflect as follows: "I shall act in such a way that, having attained omniscience, I may cause them to realize the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Then, having performed offerings, praises, and gifts to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he should bring forth the Noble Prayer of Excellent Conduct (*Āryabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna*).
Thereupon, he engages in the accumulation of the entire equipment of merit and wisdom, which has emptiness and compassion as its very core.

Thus it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti*: "In a bodhisattva who sees things as they truly are, great compassion for sentient beings arises. And he thinks: 'I must bring about this entrance into meditative concentration and the seeing of all phenomena as they truly are for the sake of all sentient beings.'"
"Being impelled by that great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he fulfills the three trainings—higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom—and awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

This very path of the Bodhisattvas, which proceeds through the union of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-yuganaddha*), is such that even while perceiving ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they do not sever conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

And not severing conventional reality, with great compassion as their precursor, they engage in activities for the benefit of sentient beings while remaining free from cognitive error (*aviparyasta*).
It is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*: "How does a bodhisattva become skilled in the Mahāyāna?
Here, a bodhisattva trains in all the trainings, yet does not apprehend the path of training."
And that which one trains in, that too one does not apprehend;
and he who trains, him too one does not apprehend;
yet, with that as its cause, that as its source, and that as its condition, one does not fall into the view of annihilationism.
And it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti*: "What is the practice of the bodhisattvas?
It is whatever bodily action of the bodhisattvas there may be, and whatever vocal action of the bodhisattvas there may be..."
Whatever mental action there may be, it all proceeds with regard for all sentient beings, because it is preceded by great compassion.
"The sovereignty of great compassion arises from the resolute intention for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings. Having such an intention for their welfare, he perceives:
"This practice must be undertaken by me, bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings."
His practice is the contemplation of the aggregates as being like an illusion, yet he does not long for the abandonment of the aggregates.
His practice is the contemplation of the elements as being like venomous serpents, yet he does not long for the abandonment of the elements.
His practice is the contemplation of the sense-bases as being like an empty village, yet he does not long for the abandonment of the sense-bases.

The practice of contemplating form as being like a mass of foam does not cause one to abandon the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s form-body; the practice of contemplating sensation as being like a bubble does not cause one to cease the application of accomplishing the bliss of the Tathāgata’s meditations, concentrations, and attainments;
and the practice of contemplating perception as being like a mirage does not constitute a failure to accomplish the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
"The practice is the contemplation of conditioned phenomena as being like a plantain tree, yet it is not the non-practice of the formative activities (*saṃskāra*) of the Buddha-qualities.

The practice is the contemplation of consciousness as being like an illusion, yet it is not the non-practice of accomplishing the actions of body, speech, and mind preceded by primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Such is the detailed explanation.
In this way, the practice consisting of wisdom and skillful means is to be understood throughout the infinite sūtras.
In this regard, even if the practice of skillful means (*upāya*) is not possible during the state of supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*),

at the time of practicing skillful means, because the bodhisattva is free from cognitive distortion (*aviparyasta*) like a magician, there indeed exists the path that proceeds by the union of wisdom and skillful means, which follows upon the application of supramundane knowledge and consists in the non-adherence to the ultimate reality of things as they truly are.
And in the *Āryakṣayamatinirdeśa*, the path that proceeds by yoking together wisdom and skillful means should be understood through the inexhaustibility of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Thus, as a bodhisattva constantly and respectfully cultivates wisdom and skillful means through practice over a long period of time according to this sequence, twelve distinct stages (*avasthā*) arise.
These very stages are established as "grounds" (*bhūmi*) in the sense of being the foundation for ever-higher qualities.
From the stage of practice through aspiration up to the Buddha-stage:
therein, as long as one does not directly realize the selflessness of persons and phenomena,
there is merely a more firm aspiration.

When one cultivates reality through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), such that one cannot be shaken even by Māra and others, then, due to that firm resolute conviction, the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) is established.

Even while abiding on this stage, the bodhisattva, though still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), has transcended all the calamities of the foolish and is endowed with qualities such as incalculable concentrations (*samādhi*), dhāraṇīs, liberations (*vimokṣa*), and superknowledges (*abhijñā*), as described in the *Āryaratnamegha*.
It is recited:
"And by means of the four stages of this very [insight]—namely, the weak, the medium, the intense, and the most intense—the four aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are established.
For instance, when a slightly clear light of knowledge arises for one who is analyzing external objects, then there occurs the aid to penetration called 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*)."

And this is called the "attainment of light" (*ālokalabdha*) samādhi within this Mahāyāna. However, when that very light of knowledge becomes moderately clear, it then becomes the aid to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) named "summit" (*mūrdhan*).
And this is called the "increased light" concentration (*vṛddhāloka-samādhi*).

However, when a clearer light of knowledge arises in which external objects do not appear, then, because one abides in representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), it becomes the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) named "patience" (*kṣānti*).
And this is called "partially entered" meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
because one has entered into the non-perception of the aspect of the apprehended object (*grāhya*).

However, when one cultivates non-dual cognition (*advayajñāna*) devoid of the aspects of both the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhaka*), then it becomes the aid to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) known as the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*agradharma*).
And that samādhi is called "uninterrupted" because one enters into reality immediately after it;
this, first of all, is the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
The other stages, however, are established as being fulfilled by eleven factors in brief.
Among them, the first stage is established as being fulfilled by the factor of the initial realization of the reality of the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
