For when, immediately after the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), there arises for the very first time a supramundane, extremely clear cognition that is free from all conceptual proliferation and directly realizes the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena;
At that time, through the entry into the state of non-arising by way of rightness and thus the arising of the path of seeing, the bodhisattva enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
For this very reason, because he has for the first time realized the reality (*tattva*) previously unrealized, the bodhisattva becomes intensely joyful;
therefore, this stage is called "The Joyful" (*pramuditā*).
And herein, one hundred and twelve afflictions to be abandoned by vision are eliminated;
the remaining stages, however, have the nature of the path of cultivation.
Within those [stages], sixteen afflictions belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation are eliminated.

And on this stage, because the Bodhisattva awakens to the realization of the *dharmadhātu* and acts for the sake of others as if it were for his own sake, the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) becomes preeminent.

Furthermore, even though that Bodhisattva has realized reality, as long as he is unable to abide in constant situational awareness regarding subtle transgressions and lapses, it remains the first stage (*bhūmi*).
But when he is able [to do so],
then, this limb being fulfilled, the second stage is established for him.
For this very reason, on this stage, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) becomes even more predominant due to the non-occurrence of even subtle transgressions or lapses.
Because it is free from the stains of all immorality, this stage is called "The Immaculate" (Vimalā).
He dwells in constant situational awareness regarding even subtle transgressions and lapses.
As long as he is unable to attain all mundane meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) and to retain the meaning of the teachings exactly as they were heard, he remains in the second stage alone.
When he is able [to fulfill that factor],
then the third stage is established upon the completion of that factor.

And on this stage, because the bodhisattva endures all suffering for the sake of attaining the retention of what has been heard and for the realization of all worldly meditative concentrations, [it is so designated].
The perfection of patience becomes even more predominant.
Because of the attainment of those meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), this stage produces an immeasurable, supramundane radiance of knowledge; thus, it is called "The Radiant" (*Prabhākarī*).

Although he has attained all worldly meditative concentrations, as long as he is unable to dwell extensively in the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) as they have been attained, and is unable to maintain equanimity of mind toward all meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), [he remains in this stage].
That much constitutes the third stage;
however, when he is able [to fulfill it], then the fourth stage is established upon the completion of that factor.

In this stage, because the bodhisattva dwells constantly with the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) for the sake of transcending the discursive proliferation of body, speech, and mind, [it is so called].
The perfection of vigor becomes preeminent.

And because the flames of the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣadharma), which are capable of burning away the fuel of all afflictions, have arisen, this stage is called "The Radiant" (arciṣmatī).
He dwells constantly in those factors conducive to awakening.

As long as, while cultivating the truths, one is unable to turn the mind away from facing toward cyclic existence and toward facing toward nirvāṇa, and is unable to cultivate the factors conducive to awakening embraced by skillful means,
that is the fourth stage.
But when he is able [to do so], then, with this limb being fulfilled, the fifth stage is established.

For this very reason, because the cultivation of the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣa) embraced by skillful means is mastered through great hardship by one who practices it, it is called "Very Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).
And in this stage, due to the frequent cultivation of the aspects of the Noble Truths, the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā) becomes even more predominant.
He dwells extensively in the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣa) embraced by skillful means (upāya).

As long as he is unable to enter the signless dwelling (animittavihāra) with a mental continuum accompanied by world-weariness (nirveda) through the contemplation of the process of cyclic existence (saṃsārapravṛtti), it is the fifth stage (bhūmi).
When he is able to do so, being perfected in this factor, the sixth stage is established.
And because this Bodhisattva dwells in the cultivation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), his perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) becomes even more preeminent.

Precisely because the perfection of wisdom has become so much more preeminent, he stands facing all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) on this stage; therefore, it is called "Facing" (*Abhimukhī*).
He becomes one who has attained the dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra*).
As long as one is unable to enter the flawless dwelling in the signless (*animitta-vihāra*), it remains the sixth stage (*bhūmi*);
when one is able to do so, this limb being perfected, it is established as the seventh stage.

On this stage as well, the bodhisattva penetrates all signs by means of the signless, yet does not contradict conventional usage established by signs. Therefore, on this stage, the perfection of skillful means becomes even more predominant. And because it is closely joined to the path of effortless spontaneity, this stage is called "Far-Reaching" (dūraṅgamā), as it has gone very far.
He dwells in the signless without interruption. As long as he is unable to enter the signless dwelling that flows effortlessly, it is the seventh stage;
when he is able, this limb being perfected, it is established as the eighth stage.
And on this stage, because of the effortless application to the side of wholesome qualities, the perfection of aspiration becomes preeminent;
because it is unshakable due to the absence of effort toward signs, this stage is called "The Immovable" (*acalā*).
Thus, he dwells in the signless state without effort (*anābhoga*).

As long as he is not yet able to master the teaching of all phenomena in all their aspects through various distinctions such as synonyms and etymologies, it is the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). When he is able to do so, because this limb is perfected, it is established as the ninth stage.

And on this stage, because the bodhisattva attains the distinction of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and is endowed with the distinction of the power of wisdom, the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) becomes even more preeminent. Because of his skill in teaching the Dharma in all its aspects and his attainment of a faultless distinction of intelligence, it is called the Stage of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*). On this stage, he becomes an obtainer of the fourfold analytical knowledge.

As long as one is unable to manifest Buddha-fields, assemblies, and so forth, nor to perform the perfect enjoyment of the Dharma and the maturation of sentient beings, it remains the ninth stage (*bhūmi*). But when one is able to do so, this factor being perfected, it is established as the tenth stage.

And on this [stage], because of the Bodhisattva’s possession of a specific excellence of knowledge for the sake of maturing sentient beings through emanations and other means, the perfection of knowledge becomes even more predominant. And because it rains the Dharma upon infinite world-systems through clouds of Dharma-teachings, it is called the "Cloud of Dharma" (dharmameghā).
There is also a presentation of the stages by means of other arrangements, such as the complete purification of the aggregates.

It has not been written here for fear of excessive prolixity. That stage is the tenth bhūmi, during which one, although having attained mastery over emanations and so forth, is still unable to produce an unattached and unimpeded knowledge regarding all objects of knowledge in all their aspects.
When one is able to do so, then, this limb being perfected, the stage of a Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*) is established. This establishment of the stages is taught in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*.

And because this stage of a Buddha reaches the ultimate limit of excellence in all aspects and in every perfection, there is no other higher state beyond it; therefore, there is no further establishment of stages after that.
Thus,
even by the Buddhas it is not possible to describe all the aspects of the classification of the qualities of this Buddha-ground,
because it is immeasurable.
But how [should it be practiced] by those such as ourselves?
As it is said in the noble Gaṇḍavyūha (Bhk 200):

"Even a Buddha, though he gazes upon them, cannot reach the limit of even a single portion of the qualities of the Self-Existent One; for the qualities of a Buddha are indeed inconceivable. This much can be said in brief.
Having reached the ultimate limit of the excellence of the fulfillment of his own and others' welfare,

and having attained the finality of the removal of all defects, the Blessed Buddha abides in the *dharmakāya* and, through the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, performs the benefit of the entire world without effort for as long as *saṃsāra* endures.
Therefore, discerning persons should generate faith in the Blessed Ones, who are mines of all virtues,
and they should strive in every way to fully realize those qualities.
The detailed classification of the three bodies and so forth is not written here for fear of excessive length in this treatise.

By whatever slight merit I have acquired through following this system, through the recitation of the Sūtra, and through these well-spoken words of this path for the sons of the Conquerors— by that, may the world, though currently dull-witted, quickly attain supreme intelligence.
By Kamalaśīla, at the command of the illustrious King Devarāja, this summary of the *Bhāvanākrama* has been composed.
The first *Bhāvanākrama* is completed.
2. The Second Stage of Meditation.
Homage to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful!
For those entering the method of the Mahāyāna sūtras, the stage of meditation is here briefly described.
In this regard, one who is discerning and desires to attain omniscience very swiftly must apply themselves to the causes and conditions that bring about its attainment.
For it is not logical that this omniscience should exist without a cause,
as that would entail the absurd consequence that everyone would possess omniscience at all times.
If there were a state of total independence, there would be no resistance whatsoever;
for indeed, not everyone is omniscient. Rather, since each person possesses only a limited degree of knowledge at any given time, every object is necessarily dependent upon causes.
Even omniscience is conceivable as something occurring somewhere at some time;
yet it does not exist at all times,
nor does it exist in all places.
Nothing at all exists [independently];
therefore, that [result] necessarily depends upon causes and conditions.
Furthermore, those causes and conditions must be cultivated when they are unerring and complete.
However, when one practices based on a mistaken cause, even over an extremely long period of time, the desired result will not be attained—
just like milking a horn for milk. Furthermore,
without cultivating the complete set of causes, the production of the result does not occur.
Because if even one [factor] among the seeds and so forth were absent, the fruit such as the sprout would not arise;
therefore, one who desires that fruit must cultivate all causes and conditions without error.
What are the causes and conditions for the fruit of omniscience?
It is said: one such as I, who am like one blind from birth, is unable to show them;
nevertheless, having been fully awakened by the Blessed One himself, I shall speak exactly as it was told to those to be trained, solely by means of the Blessed One’s own words.
The Blessed One spoke thus to him: “O Lord of Secrets!”
"That omniscient wisdom has compassion as its root, the thought of awakening as its cause, and skillful means as its culmination.
Therefore, those who desire to realize omniscience must train in these three: compassion, the thought of awakening, and skillful means.
Impelled by compassion, Bodhisattvas will necessarily make a vow for the sake of uplifting all sentient beings.

Therefore, having abandoned the view of a self, one should apply oneself with diligence to the accumulations of merit and wisdom, which are accomplished over a very long period of time and are exceedingly difficult to achieve.
Having entered therein, one will necessarily accomplish the complete accumulations of merit and wisdom.
When the accumulations are fully perfected, omniscience will be as if held in the palm of one's hand.
Therefore, since compassion alone is the very root of omniscience, it must be cultivated first of all.
As stated in the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*: "O Blessed One, a bodhisattva need not train in an excessive number of dharmas."
“O Blessed One, there is one dharma that a bodhisattva must thoroughly master and fully understand;
for him, all the qualities of a buddha will come to be held in the palm of his hand. What is this one dharma?”
"Namely, great compassion.
Because they are embraced by great compassion, the Blessed Buddhas remain until the very end of the realm of sentient beings, even though they have attained the perfection of all their own welfare;
they do not enter the city of nirvana, which is exceedingly peaceful, as the śrāvakas do.

Having observed sentient beings, because the Blessed Ones have utterly abandoned that city of peaceful nirvāṇa—viewing it as like a house on fire—it is precisely that great compassion which is the cause of their non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Herein, the sequence for cultivating compassion must be explained starting from the initial entry.
Now, by means of the cultivation of equanimity, one must first accomplish a state of even-mindedness toward all sentient beings, having cast aside both attachment and aversion.
All sentient beings desire happiness and do not desire suffering.

Furthermore, in this beginningless saṃsāra, there is no sentient being who has not been one's relative hundreds of times; when reflecting upon this, what distinction could there be [between oneself and others]?
"In that case, attachment would arise toward some and aversion toward others; therefore, I must cultivate equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings.
With such a mental orientation, beginning with those who are neutral, one should cultivate equanimity of mind toward friends and enemies alike.
Then, having established equanimity of mind toward all sentient beings, one should cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Having drenched the continuum of the mind with the water of loving-kindness and made it like fertile golden soil, the sowing of the seed of compassion (*karuṇā*) will proceed very extensively with ease.
Thereafter, having perfumed the continuum of the mind with loving-kindness, one should cultivate compassion.
And that compassion has the aspect of the desire to eliminate the suffering of all afflicted sentient beings;
because all sentient beings in the three worlds are, as the case may be, utterly tormented by the three types of suffering, it should be cultivated toward all sentient beings for their sake.
And thus, those who are not even capable of acting as agents are described in reality as being submerged in various long-lasting sufferings such as burning;
likewise, the hungry ghosts (*preta*) are also described as generally experiencing manifold suffering, their bodies withered by the fires of unbearable and intense hunger, thirst, and pain;
and even animals are clearly seen experiencing many kinds of suffering through mutual devouring, anger, killing, and violence.

Human beings as well— experiencing immeasurable suffering arising from poverty and the like, caused by mutual injury and harm born of wretchedness in the pursuit of sensual desires, and whose minds are entangled by various afflictions such as passion,

and who are submerged in the thicket of various false views— all of them are indeed exceedingly miserable, for they are like those standing on the brink of a precipice because of being the cause of suffering.
Even the gods are indeed afflicted by the suffering of universal change.
Even those gods who dwell in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) are struck by the fear and agitation of constant falling and degradation; how, then, can they be said to be happy?

Furthermore, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), characterized by karma and afflictions, dependent on causes, and having the nature of momentary disintegration, pervades the entire world.

Therefore, having realized that the entire world has entered into the midst of the blazing flames of the fire of suffering, one should reflect: "Just as suffering is unpleasant to me, so it is for others as well. Thinking, "Alas!
These dear beings of mine are suffering; how might they be freed from that suffering? one should regard their suffering as one's own.

One should cultivate compassion—which takes the form of the desire to ward off that [suffering]—at all times, both during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and throughout all activities, toward all sentient beings.
First, it should be cultivated by observing those on the side of friends who have previously experienced the various kinds of suffering described above.

Then, by means of the equality of all beings, one should cultivate it toward those in the neutral category, reflecting with the thought: "All sentient beings are indeed my own kinsmen," while perceiving no distinction between them.

When that compassion has come to function equally toward those on the side of friends as it does toward others, then one should cultivate it toward all sentient beings in the ten directions. When compassion— characterized by the desire to rescue from suffering one's own self, which is as dear as a beloved suffering child— arises spontaneously and functions equally toward all sentient beings,
then it is perfected.
And one receives the designation "great compassion.
First of all, the cultivation of loving-kindness directed toward the class of friends takes the form of a desire for their association with happiness.
This compassion should also be cultivated toward enemies who are dispersed one by one;
when practiced in this manner, that compassion gradually gives rise, by its own natural force, to the desire to uplift all sentient beings.
Therefore, having cultivated root compassion, one should cultivate the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
That bodhicitta, moreover, is twofold: the conventional and the ultimate.

Among these, the conventional is the first arousal of the thought of enlightenment, which takes the form of the desire for unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening, having made a vow out of compassion to uplift all sentient beings, thinking: "May I become a Buddha for the benefit of the world."
Nevertheless, according to the procedure shown in the *Śīlaparivarta*, a bodhisattva should generate the thought [of awakening] toward those who abide in the vows but lack wisdom.
Having thus generated the conventional thought of awakening, one should strive for the sake of generating the ultimate thought of awakening;
and that has the ultimate as its sphere.
It is stainless,
immovable, and unwavering, like the steady stream of a lamp in a windless place.

Its accomplishment, however, will come about through constantly and respectfully practicing the cultivation of the yoga of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) over a long period of time.

As it is said in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*: "Maitreya, all the mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas of the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas should be known as the fruit of calm abiding and insight."
“Because those two encompass all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) must always be practiced by all yogis.
Regarding this very point, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Ārya-saṃdhinirmocana*:
‘I have shown various meditative absorptions for the disciples (*śrāvaka*s), the bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgatas.’”
"All of these should be understood as being comprised within calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
By the cultivation of calm abiding alone, there is no abandonment of the obscurations for yogins; it results merely in the temporary suppression of the afflictions (kleśa)."
Since the abandonment of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) is impossible in the absence of the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*), the destruction of the latent dispositions will not occur.

Therefore, it is said in that very *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*: "By means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there is the suppression of the afflictions (*kleśa*); but by means of wisdom, one utterly strikes down the latent dispositions."
Also in the *Āryasamādhirājasūtra*:
"Even if one should cultivate meditative concentration in the world, if one does not eliminate the notion of a self,"

Furthermore, it is said: "The afflictions of one who contemplates the dharmas of selflessness, if he does not cultivate them after such contemplation, will flare up again—just like the cultivation of meditative concentration by Udraka here. That [contemplation] is the cause for attaining the fruit of nirvāṇa; any other cause does not lead to peace. Thus it was stated.

In the Bodhisattvapiṭaka it is also said: "Those who, without hearing these dharma-discourses of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and without hearing the noble Dharma of the Vinaya, take satisfaction in mere meditative concentration alone—having fallen into conceit through the power of egoism—are not liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair; they are not liberated from the saṃsāra of the six realms of existence, nor are they liberated even from the mass of suffering."
Referring to them, the Tathāgata has said thus: "But one whose stream of hearing is favorable toward another shall be liberated from old age and death.
Therefore, desiring the arising of pure knowledge by abandoning all obscurations, one should cultivate wisdom while established in calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Thus it is also spoken in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*:

"By being established in ethical discipline (*śīla*), one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*); from the attainment of meditative concentration, there arises the cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*);
from wisdom, pure knowledge (*jñāna*) arises; and for one whose knowledge is pure, there is the perfection of ethical discipline.
Thus it is said in the *Āryamahāyānaśraddhābhāvanāsūtra*: "O son of good family..."
"Noble son, I shall not say that the Mahāyāna faith of Bodhisattvas will arise in any way whatsoever within the Mahāyāna if wisdom is not established."

By this method as well, whatever faith in the Mahāyāna arises for Bodhisattvas toward the Mahāyāna, it should all be understood as having arisen from the thorough contemplation of the meaning of the Dharma with an undistracted mind.
Without calm abiding (*śamatha*), the yogi’s mind is distracted toward sense objects by mere insight (*vipaśyanā*) alone.
Like a lamp situated in the midst of wind, it does not become steady;
therefore, the light of knowledge does not become very clear.
Consequently, both must be practiced equally.

Therefore, it is also said in the *Ārya-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*: "The *tathāgatagotra* is not seen by the *śrāvakas*, because their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is excessive and their wisdom (*prajñā*) is deficient; however, the *bodhisattvas* see it, though not clearly."
"Because of the excess of wisdom and the deficiency of meditative concentration [in that state],
whereas the Tathāgata perceives everything due to being endowed with the equal union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Furthermore, by the power of calm abiding, the mind does not waver from the winds of conceptualization, like a lamp in a windless place."
But by means of insight (*vipaśyanā*), because all stains of wrong views are abandoned, it cannot be shattered by others.
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"One becomes unshakable through the power of tranquility (*śamatha*); one becomes like a mountain through insight."
Thus it has been said. Therefore, the practice of both is established.

In this regard, at the outset, that yogi must now cultivate the equipment for serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) in order to achieve serenity and insight easily and swiftly. Among these, what is the equipment for serenity?
dwelling in a favorable location,
having few desires, and contentment;
The avoidance of excessive activity,
purity of ethical discipline, and the abandonment of conceptual constructions such as desire;
in this regard, a location endowed with five qualities should be known as conducive.

It is "well-obtained" because clothing, food, and so forth are acquired without difficulty; it is a "good location" because it is free from the instability caused by wicked people, enemies, and the like;
it is a "good land" because it is a region free from disease.
It is a "good friend" because of his friendship, virtuous conduct, and impartiality;
it is "suitable" because it is filled with many people by day and is quiet at night. What is fewness of desire?

Contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is the lack of attachment to the excellence or abundance of robes and other requisites. What is contentment? It is the constant satisfaction with obtaining even inferior robes and so forth. (Bhk 207)
What is the avoidance of excessive activity?
It is the avoidance of evil deeds such as buying and selling,
and the avoidance of excessive intimacy with either householders or renunciants.
And the avoidance of [relying on] medicinal preparations, astrological constellations, and the like.
What is the purity of ethical discipline (*śīlaviśuddhi*)?

It is the non-violation of the training precepts regarding both types of prohibitions: those that are naturally reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*) and those that are reprehensible by convention (*pratikṣepasāvadya*).
Even when a transgression occurs through negligence, one should very quickly practice according to the Dharma with remorse;
furthermore, regarding any statement that one is unfit to remedy a *pārājika* offense within the *śrāvaka* vows, there must be remorse for that as well,
followed by the mental resolve never to repeat it.

Whatever action has been performed by the mind, because one contemplates the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) within that very mind— due to the cultivation of the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena— that alone should be called the purification of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*). This, however, is to be understood from the Noble Ajātaśatru’s Dispelling of Remorse (*Āryājātaśatrukaukṛtyavinodana*).
Therefore, having eliminated remorse, one should apply oneself to meditative cultivation.
Even regarding sensual pleasures, one should eliminate conceptual attachment toward them by reflecting upon the various faults that arise both in this life and in future births.
To this extent, whether things within the cycle of existence are pleasant or unpleasant, they are all subject to destruction and are unstable.

One must eliminate all conceptual constructions by reflecting: "Since there will certainly be a separation from all those things and from me before long, how could attachment and the like toward them arise?
What is the equipment for insight (*vipaśyanā*)?
It is reliance upon a virtuous friend (*satpuruṣa*).
The pursuit of great learning and appropriate mental attention.
If one asks, "What kind of virtuous person should one rely upon in that regard? it is one who is learned and whose speech is clear.
He is compassionate and capable of renunciation.
In this regard, what is the pursuit of great learning?
It is the respectful hearing of the twelvefold teaching of the Blessed One’s Dharma, including both the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Thus, it is stated in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*: "Not hearing the teachings of the noble ones at will is indeed an obstacle to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
In that same text: "And insight arises from the cause of pure vision produced by hearing and reflection.
Also, in the *Āryanārāyaṇaparipṛcchā*: "Wisdom manifests in one who possesses learning."
"The afflictions of one who possesses wisdom are pacified. Thus it has been said; thus it has been said.
What is appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*)?

When a Bodhisattva possesses a well-determined understanding of sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and sūtras of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), and is free from doubt, there will be a single-minded certainty regarding meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Otherwise, one who stands upon a vehicle shaken by doubt—like a person standing in the middle of a crossroads—will have no certain conviction whatsoever.
Furthermore, the yogi should always avoid fish, meat, and the like, and should eat only a fixed measure of food that is not disagreeable.
In that manner, a bodhisattva who has accumulated all the provisions for calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) should enter into cultivation.

Therein, first of all, at the time of cultivation, the yogi—having completed all his necessary duties and having voided urine and excrement—should remain in a place free from harsh sounds and the like, which is agreeable to the mind, and resolve: "I must establish all sentient beings upon the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."

Having brought forth great compassion with the intention of uplifting the entire world, and having prostrated with the five limbs to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions, one should place the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas before oneself on a cloth painting or elsewhere as appropriate; then, having performed worship and praise for them according to one's inclination, one should confess one's own misdeeds.
Having rejoiced in the merit of the entire world,

and having seated himself on a very soft and comfortable seat in the full-lotus posture of the Lord Vairocana or in the half-lotus posture, he should fix his eyes neither too wide open nor too closed upon the tip of his nose;
then, holding his body straight— neither too slumped nor too rigid— and with mindfulness turned inward, he should sit down.
Then one should keep the shoulders level;
the head should be kept steady, neither raised nor lowered, nor tilted to one side. Rather, the nose should be aligned with the navel.
The teeth and lips should be placed gently;
the tongue should be placed at the root of the upper teeth.
Furthermore, inhalation and exhalation should be performed without sound, neither coarse nor hurried.
However, one should act in such a way that [the breaths] enter or exit very slowly and without effort, so as not to be perceived.
In this regard, calm abiding (*śamatha*) must first be accomplished;
for when distractions toward external objects have ceased, the state of the mind remaining within its internal object, flowing spontaneously with joy and pliancy, is called calm abiding.
The investigation of reality at the time of taking that very same calm abiding as an object is insight (vipaśyanā).
As it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*: "Calm abiding is one-pointedness of mind; insight is the discernment of reality."
In the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana* as well: "Bhagavān, how is there the thorough seeking of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and skill in insight (*vipaśyanā*)? It is said: 'Maitreya, [it is as follows]...'"
I have established the formal arrangement of the Dharma;
namely, those categories— sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa— which were proclaimed for the Bodhisattvas,
having been heard and retained by those Bodhisattvas.
Having practiced the recitation, having examined it thoroughly with the mind, and having penetrated it well through insight, he, alone and dwelling in seclusion, [should apply himself].
Withdrawn within,

having brought to mind those very same dharmas as they were well-considered, one attends continuously with mental attention to that very internal state of mind by means of which the mental attention was performed.
Having entered in that manner and remained there many times, whatever arising of physical pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*) and mental pliancy (*cittaprasrabdhi*) exists therein is called *śamatha*.
Thus, the bodhisattva undertakes the search for *śamatha*;
by means of that, physical pliancy [is attained].
And there is tranquility of mind. Having attained these, they remain right there;
having abandoned mental distraction, they contemplate within themselves the reflection that is the object of meditative concentration (samādhi), which is the very dharma as it was contemplated.
One becomes resolved upon such a reflection within the range of meditative concentration;
that is the discernment, thorough investigation, conceptualization, examination, and patient acceptance regarding the object to be known.
The specific aspect of desire is vision,
and that which is attainment is insight (vipaśyanā).
And thus it is said that this is the bodhisattva’s skill in insight (*vipaśyanā-kausalya*):

"In that regard, a yogi desiring to accomplish calm abiding (*śamatha*) should first understand that the entirety of the teaching— the discourses (*sūtra*), verses (*geya*), and so forth— is directed toward suchness (*tathatā*) and inclines toward suchness."
"Inclined toward suchness" means that one should establish the mind upon all things by way of inclusion therein.
To this extent—in whatever manner—one should establish the mind upon the aggregates and so forth, which constitute the inclusion of all phenomena.
To this extent, the mind should be established upon an image of the Buddha as it has been seen or heard.
As it is said in the *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"The Lord of the World is serene in every way with a body of golden hue;
the Bodhisattva whose mind operates here upon this object of focus is called 'one who is concentrated' (*samāhita*). Thus it was stated.
Likewise, having placed the mind upon whatever desired object there may be, one should place the mind continuously higher and higher right there.
Having established the mind there, one should examine it in this very way.
One should examine: "Does it grasp the object well, or does it sink, or is it distracted by the influx of external objects?

In that regard, if the mind has sunk due to being overcome by sloth and torpor, or if there is a suspicion of sinking upon observation, then at that time one should attend to a joyful object, such as an image of the Buddha, or cultivate the perception of light.
Then, having stilled the sinking, one should act in such a way that the mental focus upon that very same object becomes a very clear vision.

When, however, the mind does not perceive the object of focus with extreme clarity— like one born blind, or like a person who has entered darkness, or like one with eyes closed— it should then be understood as sunken (*līna*).

When there is a running toward external forms and so forth through the conceptualization of their qualities, or through mental wandering, or through desire for objects previously experienced, resulting in mental agitation (*auddhatya*) or the perception of a suspicion of agitation, then [one should contemplate] that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, suffering, and so forth, as an object for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
One should attend to this:
then, having pacified distraction, the elephant of the mind must be bound to that very pillar of the focal object with the rope of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
When neither lethargy nor excitement occurs, one should observe the tranquility and stability of the mind through that focal object.
Then, by relaxing the mental effort (*ābhoga*), one may remain for as long as desired through equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For one who has thus cultivated calm abiding (*śamatha*), there will arise pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of both that body and the mind;
the mind will come under its own control regarding any object as desired.
Then it should be understood that calm abiding (śamatha) has been accomplished.
Having thus accomplished calm abiding, one should cultivate insight (vipaśyanā).
And one should reflect in this way: "Every word of the Blessed One is well-spoken."
Whether directly or indirectly, that which manifests the direct perception of reality and is devoted solely to reality will result in liberation from the entire web of views,
just as darkness is dispelled by the arising of light when there is knowledge of reality.
Through calm abiding (*śamatha*) alone, the purification of knowledge will not occur.
Furthermore, there will be no dispelling of the darkness of obscurations;
rather, through wisdom (*prajñā*), by means of the correct cultivation of reality, the purification of knowledge will occur.
It is by wisdom alone that reality is understood, and it is by wisdom alone that obscurations are correctly abandoned.
Therefore, I must abide in calm abiding (*śamatha*) and seek reality (*tattva*) through wisdom (*prajñā*). One should reflect that satisfaction should not be found in calm abiding alone.
And if one asks, "What kind of reality is it? [the answer follows].
That which is ultimately empty of all things, persons, phenomena, and self is realized through the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and not otherwise.
As it is said in the *Ārya-saṃdhinirmocana*: "O Bhagavat..."
"By which perfection does a bodhisattva grasp the lack of intrinsic nature of phenomena?
"Avalokiteśvara,
it is grasped by the perfection of wisdom."
Thus,
having established oneself in calm abiding (śamatha), one should cultivate wisdom (prajñā).
In that regard, the yogi should investigate as follows:
A person (pudgala) is not perceived as distinct from the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana);
nor is the person the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the aggregates and so forth.
However, those aggregates and so forth are impermanent.
Because the person (*pudgala*) possesses multiple intrinsic natures, and because it is imagined by others as being eternal and of a single form,
it is also not logical for an ineffable person to have substantial reality (*vastutva*) in terms of either identity with or difference from [the aggregates],
since there is no other possible mode for that which exists as a real entity.
Therefore, one should reflect that this notion of "I" and "mine" in the world is merely an illusion;
likewise, the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) should be understood in this way.
Briefly stated, "phenomena" refers to the five aggregates and the twelve sense bases.
And there are the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Among these, those which are the material forms of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are not, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), distinct from the aspects of the mind (*cittākāra*).
When that [object] is analyzed down to its atoms, even those atoms, upon being examined for their intrinsic nature part by part, lack any apprehension of a definitive intrinsic nature. Therefore,

due to the force of beginningless attachment to false forms and so forth, the mind of the ignorant alone appears as an external manifestation of forms and so forth— as if it were discrete— just like the appearance of forms perceived in a dream.
From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should investigate that form and the other aggregates are not distinct from the aspects of the mind (*cittākāra*).
Thus, one should contemplate that these three realms are mind-only (*cittamātra*).

Having thus determined that the mind alone constitutes the designation of all phenomena (*dharmaprajñapti*) and having examined it therein, one comes to have examined the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena; and so too the intrinsic nature of the mind itself.
He reflects in this way:
"It is not logical for even the mind to be ultimately real.
For when the mind itself appears in various forms upon grasping the aspects of form and so forth, which have a false nature,"
In that case, where could reality exist?
Just as form and so forth are false, so too is the mind false, because it is not distinct from them.

Just as form and other phenomena, by virtue of their variegated appearances, do not possess a nature that is either one or many, so too the mind—being non-different from them—does not possess a nature that is either one or many.
Therefore, the mind is indeed comparable in its essential nature to an illusion and the like.
One should investigate that just as it is with the mind, so all phenomena as well are exactly like illusions in their essential nature.

When he thus examines the intrinsic nature of the mind with that wisdom, from the perspective of ultimate reality, he does not apprehend the mind internally, nor does he apprehend it externally, nor does he apprehend it as neither.
One does not apprehend even the past mind, one does not apprehend the future,
nor does one apprehend the present.
Furthermore, the mind, when arising, does not come from anywhere, nor does it go anywhere when ceasing;
for the mind is ungraspable, indefinable, and formless.
What is the nature of that which exists as indefinable, ungraspable, and formless?
Thus it is said in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*: "Kāśyapa, when the mind is thoroughly sought, it is not found."
That which is not obtained is not apprehended,
and that which is not apprehended is neither past nor future.
"Nor [is it] the present," and so forth in detail.
Thus, when examined in this way, one does not perceive a beginning of the mind.
One does not perceive an end, nor does one perceive a middle.
Just as the mind is without end or middle, so too should one understand all phenomena to be without end or middle.
Having thus understood that very mind to be without end or middle, one does not apprehend any intrinsic nature of the mind whatsoever.
Furthermore, whatever mind is examined, one penetrates that too as empty.
When penetrating it thus, one does not perceive even the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, which is the lack of intrinsic nature in the mental constructions of the mind.
Therefore, because through such wisdom there is no perception of the intrinsic nature of any phenomenon, [one sees] whether form is permanent or impermanent.
Whether empty or non-empty,
with outflows or without outflows,
arisen or unarisen.
One does not conceptualize it as "existence" or "non-existence.
Just as one does not conceptualize form (*rūpa*), so too one does not conceptualize feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), or consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is because when the substratum (*dharmin*) is unestablished, its qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) are likewise unestablished.
In that regard, how could one conceptualize?
Thus, when a yogi, examining with wisdom, does not apprehend a determination of the ultimate intrinsic nature of any entity whatsoever, [how could there be conceptualization]?
Then one enters into non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*),

and the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena is also realized; this occurs for one who, having investigated the intrinsic nature of things with wisdom, does not engage in mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
If one cultivates merely the abandonment of mental attention, one's conceptual construction will never cease,
nor will there be an awakening to the lack of intrinsic nature.

Because of the absence of the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*), the Blessed One has said that when the fire of correct knowledge of reality as it is arises through such right investigation—like fire produced by churning the *araṇi* wood—the tree of conceptual construction is burned away.

Likewise, it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*: "Being thus skilled in [identifying] defects, he applies himself to yoga for the sake of the departure from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and for the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."

Abounding in the cultivation of emptiness, wherever his mind extends or wherever his mind finds delight, he thoroughly investigates those very places as to their intrinsic nature and penetrates them as empty.
Examining that very mind as well, he penetrates it as empty; and even the mind by which he examines, when thoroughly sought, he penetrates as empty of intrinsic nature.
Examining in this way, he attains yoga in signlessness.
Thus it occurs.
By this, however, he shows that the entry into signlessness is preceded by thorough investigation;
it is merely the relinquishing of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Without having analyzed the intrinsic nature of things through wisdom, and without conceiving of an entry into non-conceptuality,
he demonstrates it most clearly.
Likewise, having correctly and accurately examined the intrinsic nature of entities such as form with that wisdom, one meditates;
one does not practice meditation while remaining fixed upon form and so forth,
nor does one practice meditation while remaining between this world and the next.
Because of the non-perception of form and so forth,
it is called "non-abiding meditation.
Since one meditates on non-perception after having scrutinized with wisdom the intrinsic nature of all things, it is called "meditation preceded by wisdom."
As it has been taught in the *Āryagaganagañja*, the *Āryaratnacūḍa*, and other sūtras:
having thus entered into the reality consisting of the selflessness of persons and phenomena,
he ceases [from further inquiry], because there is nothing else remaining to be examined or to be seen.

With a mind that is of a single flavor, inexpressible through applied and sustained thought, and flowing spontaneously, one should remain cultivating reality itself even more clearly without volitional effort;
and remaining therein, one should not distract the continuum of the mind.

When the mind is distracted outwardly by passion and other afflictions in the interim, one should recognize that distraction and, having quickly stilled the distraction through the cultivation of the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth, swiftly cause the mind to enter repeatedly into suchness (*tathatā*).
However, when one perceives that the mind is not taking delight therein, [one should apply the appropriate remedy].
Then, by seeing the virtues of meditative concentration (samādhi), one should cultivate delight in it;
and by seeing the faults in distraction, one should pacify any lack of delight.
Furthermore, when one perceives the mind to be sluggish due to its clear manifestation being overwhelmed by sloth and torpor (styāna-middha), [one should apply the appropriate remedy].
If, at that time, one suspects laxity (*laya*), one should quickly pacify it by reflecting upon an object of joy as before.
Then, one should again grasp that very same objective support of reality (*tattvālambana*) with even greater firmness.

If, at that time, one perceives the mind to have become internally excited by recollecting past laughter and play, or if one suspects agitation (*auddhatya*), then one should [pacify] the distraction by reflecting upon objects that induce a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), such as impermanence (*anityatā*).
One should pacify it.
Then, one should again exert effort toward the effortless flow of the mind within that very reality (*tattva*).

Now, when the mind arises directed toward that same reality—clearer, flowing by its own natural force, and proceeding in equilibrium because it is free from both lethargy and agitation—[one should maintain it].
At that time, because the application of effort has been relaxed, one should practice equanimity;
for if effort is applied when the mind is proceeding in equilibrium, then the mind becomes distracted.
Even when the mind is in a state of dullness,
if no mental application is made,
then because of excessive dullness, it is devoid of insight (vipaśyanā).
The mind will become like one born blind. Therefore, when the mind is sluggish, one should engage in cultivation; when it is proceeding with equanimity, one should not engage in cultivation.

And when one cultivates insight (vipaśyanā) such that wisdom becomes excessive, then because of the deficiency of calm abiding (śamatha), the mind wavers like a lamp placed in a windy spot; consequently, the vision of reality will not be clear.
Therefore, at that time, one should cultivate calm abiding.
Even when there is an excess of *śamatha*, wisdom (*prajñā*) must be cultivated.
When both are proceeding in equilibrium, one should remain without any further volitional effort for as long as no affliction of body or mind arises.

When such affliction of the body and so forth occurs, in the interim, one should view the entire world as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, or the reflection of the moon in water, and reflect as follows:
"Yet these sentient beings are afflicted in saṃsāra because they do not realize the profundity of such a Dharma. Therefore, I shall act so that they may realize that very nature of reality;
I shall act in such a way"—thinking thus, one should bring forth great compassion directed toward the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).

Then, having rested, one should again enter the *sarvadharmanirābhāsa* (non-appearance of all phenomena) samādhi in the same manner. When the mind becomes excessively weary, one should rest in that same way.
This path, however, which proceeds by the union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), takes as its object both conceptual and non-conceptual images.
In this manner, the yogi should remain cultivating reality through this sequence for one *ghaṭikā*, half a watch (*prahara*), or one full watch, or for as long as he desires.
This is the meditation on the investigation of meaning (*arthapravicaya-dhyāna*) as taught in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*.
Then, wishing to arise from meditative absorption, one should reflect thus without breaking the cross-legged posture:

"All these phenomena, while being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nonetheless remain established within the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
This being so, how could the connection between karma and its fruit and so forth be established?"
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"Entities exist conventionally; in the ultimate sense, there are no entities. Thus it has been stated.
These people of immature intellect possess perverted minds because they superimpose existence and other qualities upon things that lack intrinsic nature.

They wander for a long time in the wheel of saṃsāra; therefore, I shall fulfill the unsurpassed accumulation of merit and wisdom, and having attained the state of omniscience, I shall cause them to realize the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
One should reflect in this way:

then, gradually breaking the cross-legged posture, one should prostrate to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions, offer worship and hymns of praise to them, and make the great vow of the Noble Bhadracaryā and so forth.
Therefore, one must apply oneself to the accumulation of the entire equipment of merit, such as generosity and the rest, which have emptiness and compassion as their core.
When this is done, there will be the realization of that meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) which is endowed with the excellence of all aspects of emptiness.

As it is said in the *Āryaratnacūḍa*: “Armored with the mail of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and standing upon the ground of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), he practices the meditative concentration that realizes emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects.”
In that regard, what is emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects?

It is that which is described in detail as "not departing from generosity, not departing from ethical discipline, not departing from patience, not departing from diligence, not departing from meditative concentration, not departing from wisdom, not departing from skillful means," and so forth.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should bring all sentient beings to maturity.
Furthermore, one must certainly cultivate the roots of virtue such as giving, which are the means for manifesting the excellence of the field, the body, the vast retinue, and so forth.
For if that were not the case, to whom would the excellence of the fields and other qualities described by the Buddhas belong as a fruit?

Therefore, because that omniscient gnosis endowed with the excellence of all aspects is fulfilled through the means of giving and the rest, the Blessed One declared that this omniscient gnosis reaches its ultimate limit through skillful means.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should cultivate the means such as generosity and so forth, and not emptiness alone. As it is said in the *Āryasarvadharmavaipulya*:
"Maitreya, whoever this is..."
The complete realization of the six perfections is for the sake of the full awakening of bodhisattvas; yet those deluded persons will say this:
"A bodhisattva should train only in the perfection of wisdom; what is the use of the remaining perfections? Thus they speak.
They will think that those other perfections should be disparaged.
What do you think, Ajita?
Was that King of Kāśi lacking in wisdom when he gave his own flesh to the hawk for the sake of the dove?
Maitreya said,
"Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Those which have been taught by me, Maitreya..."
"While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, roots of merit associated with the six perfections were accumulated;
was any harm done by those roots of merit?
Maitreya replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Ajita, you yourself have for sixty kalpas perfected the perfection of giving,

for sixty kalpas the perfection of ethical discipline, for sixty kalpas the perfection of patience, for sixty kalpas the perfection of vigor, for sixty kalpas the perfection of meditation, and for sixty kalpas the perfection of wisdom."
It has been fully realized.
Regarding this, those deluded persons will say:
"Awakening is by means of a single method alone, namely the method of emptiness," and they will claim that their conduct is purified, and so forth.

When devoid of skillful means, a bodhisattva is unable to perform the works of a Buddha through wisdom alone, just like a śrāvaka; however, when supported by skillful means, he becomes capable. As it is said in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*: "For example, Kāśyapa..."
"Kings perform all their duties when supported by their ministers;
in the very same way, the wisdom of a bodhisattva performs all the works of a Buddha when supported by skillful means.
Thus it is said.
The view of the path held by Bodhisattvas is one thing, while the view of the path held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and Śrāvakas is another.
Thus, because the view of the path of non-Buddhists is associated with the misconceptions (*viparyāsa*) regarding a self and so forth, it is a path entirely devoid of wisdom in every respect.
Therefore, they do not attain liberation.
However, because the Śrāvakas lack great compassion, they are devoid of skillful means;
therefore, they become intent solely upon nirvāṇa. But the path of the Bodhisattva is considered to be endowed with both wisdom and skillful means.
Therefore, they have non-abiding nirvana as their ultimate goal.
The path of the bodhisattvas, however, is considered to be endowed with both wisdom and skillful means;
therefore, they attain non-abiding nirvana.
By the power of wisdom, one does not fall into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*);
and by the power of skillful means (*upāya*), one does not fall into nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is said in the *Āryagayāśīrṣa*: "These two are the concise paths of the bodhisattvas."
"What are these two? Namely, wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). Thus it is declared.
It is also stated in the *Āryaśrīparamādya*: (Bhk 217)
“Prajñāpāramitā is the ‘mother,’ and upāyakauśalya is the ‘father.
In the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra* it is also asked: ‘What is the bondage of bodhisattvas?’”
And what is liberation?
For a bodhisattva, grasping at the realms of existence by means of non-expedient means is bondage;
proceeding through the realms of existence by means of expedient means is liberation.
For a bodhisattva, taking hold of the states of existence devoid of wisdom is bondage;
however, proceeding through the states of existence by means of wisdom is liberation.
Indeed, wisdom that is not embraced by skillful means is bondage.
"Wisdom embraced by skillful means is liberation; skillful means not embraced by wisdom is bondage;
skillful means grasped by wisdom is liberation"—this has been explained at length.
For a bodhisattva, the exclusive cultivation of wisdom alone will result in falling into the nirvāṇa desired by the śrāvakas, which is like a bondage;
there will be no liberation through non-abiding nirvāṇa.
Therefore, wisdom devoid of skillful means is said to be a bondage for bodhisattvas.

Therefore, just as one oppressed by wind resorts to fire, a bodhisattva—because they have abandoned only the winds of cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*)—should resort to emptiness through wisdom accompanied by compassion, but it should not be realized [as a final goal] as is done by the śrāvakas.
As it is said in the *Āryadaśadharma-sūtra*: "O son of good family!..."
For example, it is just as when a certain person performs service to fire; he honors that fire and treats it with reverence.
However, even though I have honored, revered, and respected this fire, thinking "this is that very same one," he does not consider that it should be grasped with both hands.
If one asks why that is, it is because of the thought: "If I were to place it [on my lap], physical pain or mental distress might arise within me."
In the same way, although a bodhisattva also possesses the aspiration for nirvāṇa,
he does not directly realize nirvāṇa.
If one asks why that is:
"Because of that deposit, I shall realize awakening"—from such a thought [arises this].
However, even by practicing mere skillful means alone, a bodhisattva, because he has not yet transcended the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), will remain utterly bound.
Therefore, one should practice skillful means conjoined with wisdom (*prajñā*).
In this way, just as poison that has been taken hold of by a mantra becomes nectar when cultivated through the power of being embraced by wisdom, so too it is with the afflictions of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, what more need be said regarding those things such as generosity which, by their very nature, yield the fruit of higher rebirth?
As it is said in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*: "Kāśyapa, it is just as if..."

Just as poison that is counteracted by mantras and medicinal herbs does not cause death, even so, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of Bodhisattvas, because they are embraced by wisdom (*prajñā*), are unable to cause them to fall [into ruin]. Therefore, for this reason—that a Bodhisattva, through the power of skillful means (*upāya*), does not abandon cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—he does not fall into [the extreme of] nirvana.
And because, through the power of wisdom, all objective referents (*ālambana*) are abandoned, he does not fall into cyclic existence.
Therefore, the state of Buddhahood, which is non-abiding nirvāṇa, is attained.
For this reason, it is also said in the *Āryagaganagañja*: "By means of the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) are completely abandoned;
by means of the knowledge of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*), all sentient beings are not forsaken."
Thus it is said;

and in the *Ārya-saṃdhinirmocana* as well: “I have not declared that unexcelled, perfect enlightenment belongs to one who is entirely turned away from the welfare of sentient beings, nor to one who is entirely turned away from the formative activity of conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, by one desiring to attain Buddhahood, both wisdom and skillful means must be cultivated.

In that regard, even when there is no possibility of practicing the means such as generosity during the occasion of cultivating supramundane wisdom or during the state of extreme meditative concentration, whatever [wisdom] exists therein— both the wisdom of application and the subsequently attained wisdom—
then the practice of the means indeed occurs.
Therefore, wisdom and skillful means proceed simultaneously.

Furthermore, because this path of the bodhisattvas—which carries wisdom and skillful means joined together—is embraced by great compassion that gazes upon all sentient beings, it is cultivated as a supramundane path;
even at the time of exerting skillful means, giving and the other perfections are practiced without error, just like a magician.
As it is also said in the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśa*: "In that regard, what is the bodhisattva’s skillful means (*upāya*) and what is the accomplishment of wisdom (*prajñā*)?

Since the stabilization of the mind upon meditative concentration, while taking as its object great compassion that surveys sentient beings, is itself skillful means; [the rest follows as the accomplishment of wisdom]."
“For that which is the attainment of peace and perfect tranquility is wisdom (*prajñā*),” and so forth.
It is also stated in the *Māradamana-pariccheda*: “Furthermore, the superior application of the bodhisattvas exerts itself through the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*);
through the knowledge of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*), there is the gathering of all wholesome dharmas. (Bhk 219)
It is also applied [in this way]:
through the knowledge of wisdom (prajñājñāna), one applies oneself to selflessness, the absence of a sentient being, a life-force, a nourisher, and a person;
and through the knowledge of skillful means (upāyajñāna), that which is the ripening of all sentient beings is also to be applied—thus it is explained in detail.

Also in the *Āryadharmasaṃgītisūtra*: "Just as a certain magician, having previously known [the nature of his illusions], strives for the liberation of a created being, yet has no attachment to that creation."

"Having realized that the three realms of existence are like a magical creation, one who has reached the further shore of perfect awakening girds himself for the sake of the world, even though he already knows the world as it truly is. Thus, for those named Bodhisattvas, the very method of wisdom and skillful means is directed toward the goal to be accomplished; therefore, even while remaining within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through its application, [the goal] exists.
It has been stated that one may even abide in the nirvāṇa of one’s own disposition.

Having performed the cultivation of skillful means such as generosity— which have been transformed into unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, the essence of which is emptiness and great compassion— one should, for the sake of generating the ultimate bodhicitta, constantly practice the application of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) from time to time according to one's ability, as previously described.

In the *Āryagocarapariśuddhisūtra*, the benefits for bodhisattvas who act for the sake of sentient beings in all circumstances have been taught; accordingly, one should always cultivate skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*) with ever-present mindfulness.
One who cultivates such compassion, skill in means, and the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) will certainly become distinguished in this very life.
Therefore, there will be a constant vision of Buddhas and bodhisattvas even in dreams.
Various auspicious dreams will also be seen;
even the gods will provide protection out of sympathetic joy;
and at every moment, there will be an accumulation of a vast store of merit and wisdom.
The depravity of the afflictive obscurations will also be exhausted;
there will always be an abundance of physical ease and mental well-being;
and one will become beloved by many people.
Even in the body, one will not be afflicted by disease;
moreover, supreme flexibility of mind will be attained.
From that, there will be the attainment of distinguished qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Then, having gone to infinite world-systems by means of the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), he makes offerings to the Blessed Buddhas;
from them, the Dharma is also heard.
Even at the time of death, there will certainly be a vision of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
in future lives as well, one will be born in a distinguished household that is never separated from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Consequently, the equipment of merit and wisdom will be fulfilled without effort.
He will possess great wealth and a large retinue;
with sharp wisdom, he will also bring many people to spiritual maturity;
and in all births, he will have the recollection of his former lives.
Such immeasurable benefits as have arisen in other sūtras are to be understood [in this case as well].

Therefore, because such compassion, skillful means, and the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) have been cultivated constantly, with reverence, and for a long time, they gradually reach full maturity through the arising of extremely pure moments within the mental continuum; thus, like fire produced by rubbing the fire-sticks, they reach the ultimate limit of the cultivation of the correct meaning.
Having become the "going," it is the departure from the entire web of conceptual constructions of supramundane gnosis; it is the clear realization of the non-proliferated *dharmadhātu*.

Like a lamp that is stainless, motionless, and situated in a windless place, it is a motionless means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), having the nature of the selflessness of all phenomena, and directly perceiving reality (*tattva*).

The nature of the ultimate bodhicitta, which is subsumed within the path of seeing (darśanamārga), arises. Through its arising, one enters into the objective support that is the limit of phenomena (vastuparyantatā) and is born into the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
The engagement in the non-defilement of bodhisattvas;
the cessation of all worldly destinies;
and the abiding in the realization of the dharma-realm as the true nature of bodhisattvas.
The attainment of the first bodhisattva stage is the benefit; its detailed exposition is to be understood from the *Daśabhūmika* and other such texts.
This meditation, which has suchness as its object, is taught in the *Ārya-laṅkāvatāra*.
However, this [meditation] leads the bodhisattvas into the state of non-proliferation and non-conceptuality itself.
On the stage of resolute belief (*adhimukti-bhūmi*), however, engagement is established by the power of resolute belief and not through volitional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*);
but upon the manifestation of that knowledge, there is direct entry.

Likewise is the entry into the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*); immediately thereafter, on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), by means of supramundane knowledge and the subsequently attained knowledge (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
And by means of both, through the sequence of cultivating wisdom and skillful means, one purifies the most subtle and even subtler accumulated obscurations that are to be abandoned by cultivation;
thereby, for the sake of attaining ever-higher, distinguished qualities, one enters up to the limit of the Tathāgata’s gnosis by thoroughly cleansing the lower stages,
and descends into the ocean of omniscience.
It also attains the objective support of the fulfillment of the task.
Thus, the purification of the mental continuum occurs gradually; this is also stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra* and in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*. (Bhk 221)
As it has been said: "By purifying the mind through successive higher stages like gold, one awakens to the ultimate, unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Upon entering the ocean of omniscience, one becomes endowed with a mass of qualities that sustain all sentient beings, like a wish-fulfilling gem, honored as the fruit of previous vows.
Having become the very nature of great compassion, and being endowed with various effortless means, he has made all the aims of the entire world without exception through immeasurable emanations.
Having reached the ultimate limit of the excellence of the perfection of all qualities without exception,
having eliminated every stain along with the defects of latent tendencies,
he dwells as far as the very limits of the realm of sentient beings.
Thus, a discerning person, having generated faith in the Blessed Buddha, the mine of all virtues, should personally exert every effort for the sake of perfecting those qualities.
Therefore, the Blessed One has said: "This very wisdom of the Omniscient One has compassion as its root, the thought of awakening as its cause, and skillful means as its culmination.
For those who have cast far away the stains of envy and the like are never satiated by virtues, just as the ocean is never satiated by waters.
Having discerned them, they accept well-spoken words, just as joyful swans take up the milk from the waters.
Therefore, the wise have removed from their minds that which is clouded by partiality;
indeed, every well-spoken word should be accepted even from a child.
Whatever merit has been attained by me through elucidating this peerless path,
may all beings, by that merit, attain the middle path.
The *Bhāvanākrama* composed by Ācārya Kamalaśīla in the middle [of his works] is completed.
It was translated, edited, and thoroughly finalized by the Indian Upādhyāya Prajñāvarman, the Great Eye of the World, and Vandyajñānasena.
The second *Bhāvanākrama* is completed.
(Bhk 222): blank (Bhk 223) 3. The Third Stage of Cultivation (Bhāvanākrama)
The stages of meditation for those engaged in the method of the Mahāyāna sūtras are here briefly described.

In this regard, although the Blessed One has taught an immeasurable variety of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) for bodhisattvas— distinguished by categories such as the "immeasurables" (*apramāṇa*) and so forth—
nevertheless, all meditative concentrations are encompassed by calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
That very path, which proceeds by yoking together calm abiding and insight, is now described.
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"A living being [is bound] from the bond of signs and further from the bond of corruption."
"Having cultivated insight and tranquility, one is liberated.
Therefore, those who desire the abandonment of all obscurations should cultivate both tranquility and insight.
By the power of tranquility, the mind becomes unshakable with respect to its object, like a lamp placed in a windless spot.

Through insight (vipaśyanā), because of the realization of the reality of phenomena as they truly are, the light of correct knowledge arises; consequently, all obscurations are abandoned, just as darkness is dispelled by the arising of light.
For this very reason, the Blessed One has taught four objects of focus for practitioners:
the non-conceptual image, the conceptual image, [the thing itself, and the perfection].
The limit of things (*vastuparyantatā*) and the fulfillment of the task (*kāryapariniṣpatti*).

Among these, that which is focused upon by resolving upon the reflected image of all phenomena and the form of the Buddha and so forth through calm abiding (*śamatha*) is called the non-conceptual reflected image (*nirvikalpapratibimbaka*).
In that regard, it is called "non-conceptual" because there is an absence of conceptualization regarding the investigation of the true nature of reality.
It is called a "reflected image" because one focuses upon and takes as an object a reflection of the phenomena (dharmas) as they were grasped according to what was heard.
When the yogi examines that very reflected image through insight (*vipaśyanā*) for the sake of realizing reality, it is then called a "conceptual reflected image."
Because the conceptualization that discerns reality, which is characterized by insight (*vipaśyanā*), arises therein,
the yogi, while discerning the intrinsic nature of that very reflection, is like one who determines the defects present on his own face by examining the reflection of his face within a mirror.
Because of the thorough understanding of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena as they truly are:

when one penetrates suchness, which is characterized by the limit of things (*vastuparyantatā*), then, due to that understanding of the limit of things, it is called the "object of the limit of things" on the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Then, through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), as one gradually gives rise to increasingly purer moments— like the application of medicinal herbs and elixirs (*rasāyana*)— when the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) occurs and the completion of the task characterized by the abandonment of obscurations takes place, that very same gnosis on the Buddha-stage is called the objective support for the perfection of the task.
What, then, is shown by this?
Through both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), there occurs the realization of the ultimate limit of all things.
By means of that, the fulfillment of the task—characterized by the abandonment of obscurations—is attained;
and that itself is Buddhahood.

Therefore, one who seeks the attainment of Buddhahood must cultivate calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). For one who does not cultivate these two, there is neither the realization of the ultimate limit of phenomena (*vastuparyantatā*) nor the perfection of the task to be accomplished.
In this context, calm abiding is one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
"Vipaśyanā is the discernment of reality"—thus, in brief, the Blessed One has described the characteristics of śamatha and vipaśyanā in such works as the *Āryaratnamegha*.

In this regard, a yogin, established in the prerequisites for śamatha and vipaśyanā beginning with the purity of ethical discipline, should generate great compassion toward all sentient beings; having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he should apply himself to hearing, reflection, and meditation.
In that regard, first of all, at the time of cultivation, the yogi— having completed all his necessary duties and having voided urine and excrement—

should remain in a location free from thorns, harsh sounds, and the like, which is agreeable to the mind. Having resolved, "I must establish all sentient beings upon the seat of enlightenment," and having brought forth great compassion with the intention of uplifting the entire world, he should proceed.

Having prostrated with the five limbs before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions, having placed the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas upon a seat or elsewhere in front of oneself as appropriate, and having performed worship and praise for them according to one's inclination, one should confess one's own misdeeds and rejoice in the merit of the entire world.
Having sat down on a very soft and comfortable seat in the full lotus posture of the Lord Vairocana,

or in the half-lotus posture, with the eyes neither too wide open nor too closed, fixed upon the tip of the nose; and having set the body straight, neither too bent nor too rigid, one should sit with mindfulness directed inwardly.
Then one should keep the shoulders level;
the head should be kept steady, neither raised nor lowered, nor tilted to one side. Rather, the nose should be aligned with the navel.

The teeth and lips should be set gently; the tongue should be placed against the root of the upper teeth. Furthermore, inhalation and exhalation should be performed neither with sound, nor coarsely, nor hurriedly.
However, one should act so that they enter or exit without being noticed, very slowly and effortlessly.
In this regard, first of all, the yogi, having fixed the mind upon the form of the Tathāgata as it has been seen or heard, should accomplish *śamatha*.
And that form of the Tathāgata is pure like refined gold, adorned with the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*), and situated in the midst of the circle of the assembly.
While performing the welfare of sentient beings through various means, one should, by means of continuous mental attention and based on a longing for those qualities,
pacify laxity, excitement, and so forth, and meditate until one sees [the Tathāgata] as if clearly standing before one.
Then, one cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*) while examining the coming and going of that reflected image of the Tathāgata’s body.
Then, one should reflect in this way:

"Just as this reflected image of the Tathāgata’s body has come from nowhere and will go nowhere, and even while it stands, it is empty of intrinsic nature and devoid of self and what belongs to a self; in the very same way, all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, devoid of coming and going, and like reflections."

Having reflected that [all things] are devoid of the nature of existence and so forth, one should remain for as long as desired, contemplating reality with a mind that has ceased its discursive inquiry and is of a single flavor free from verbalization.

This samādhi is taught as the *pratyutpanna-buddha-saṃmukhāvasthita-samādhi* (the samādhi of standing face-to-face with the Buddhas of the present). Its benefits should be understood in detail from that very sūtra.
In this manner, there is a complete inclusion of all phenomena;
having fixed the mind upon that, one should accomplish *śamatha* through the pacification of laxity, excitement, and so forth.
Furthermore, [this is done] by means of the distinction between the material and the immaterial.
In brief, this is the summary of all phenomena (*dharma*):
therein, those comprised within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) are material;
those whose intrinsic nature consists of the aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*) are immaterial.
In that regard, fools, due to their attachment to the grasping of entities and so forth, wander in saṃsāra with perverted intellects;
for the sake of removing their perversion,
and having brought forth great compassion toward them, [one should act].
Once calm abiding (śamatha) has been accomplished, the yogi should then cultivate insight (vipaśyanā) for the sake of attaining reality.
Insight is defined as the discernment of reality (bhūta-pratyavekṣaṇā),
and reality, moreover, is the selflessness of persons and phenomena (pudgala-dharma-nairātmya).
In that regard, the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is the state of the aggregates being devoid of a self and what belongs to a self;
the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is the fact that those very [aggregates] are like an illusion.
Therein, the practitioner should investigate in this way.
