First of all, there is no person (pudgala) distinct from form and the other aggregates, because such a thing does not appear [to cognition]; rather,
the notion "I" arises only with respect to form and the rest.
Nor is the person (pudgala) of the same nature as the aggregates such as form;
for those [aggregates] such as form possess an impermanent and manifold nature,
whereas the person is imagined by others to have a permanent and unitary form.
Nor is it logical for a person who is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from [the aggregates] to possess substantial reality,
because there is no other possible mode of existence for that which is substantially real.
Therefore, this conviction of "I" and "mine" held by the world— which has fallen into such a state— is nothing but a false delusion.

Then, one should also investigate material phenomena (*rūpin*) in order to realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*): "Do these exist as ultimate realities apart from the mind, or does it rather appear that the mind itself manifests in the appearance of form and so forth, just like the appearances in the state of dreaming?
Examining them down to their atomic constituents, he [finds]—
Examining atoms part by part, one does not perceive them;
thus, not perceiving them, one turns away from the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence regarding them.
One enters into the realization that the triple world is mind-only, and not otherwise.
Moreover, it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra*:
"One analyzes substance down to its atoms and does not conceptualize form at all;
yet one does not gain confidence in the establishment of 'mind-only' due to wrong views."

It occurs to him: "Due to the power of an attachment to false forms and so forth since beginningless time, it is the mind itself that appears to the foolish as an appearance of forms and so forth externally and as if separate, just like the appearance of forms perceived in a dream."
Therefore, the triple world is mind-only.

Having thus determined that the designation of all phenomena is mind alone, and having examined it therein, he considers that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena has been examined; he likewise investigates the intrinsic nature of the mind itself in this way:
The mind, too, is ultimately unarisen like an illusion.
For when the mind itself appears in various forms by assuming the aspects of form and so forth— which have a false nature— then,
since it is not distinct from them, how could its reality exist, just as it does not for form and the rest?

Just as form and other phenomena, by virtue of their variegated aspects, do not possess a nature that is either one or many, so too the mind—being non-different from them—does not possess a nature that is either one or many.
Furthermore, when the mind arises, it does not come from anywhere;
nor, when ceasing, does it go anywhere.
Nor is its arising from itself, from another, or from both ultimately tenable.
Therefore, the mind is indeed like an illusion;
and as the mind is, so too all phenomena are, like illusions, unarisen in the ultimate sense.
Even the mind with which the yogi examines, when its own intrinsic nature is scrutinized, is not perceived.
Thus, wherever the yogi’s mind may extend toward an object of focus, by scrutinizing the intrinsic nature of each, he does not perceive even that intrinsic nature.
When he does not perceive it, then, having investigated every entity, he [realizes their lack of self-nature].
Having understood that [the body] is as essence-less as the trunk of a plantain tree,
he turns his mind away from it;
then, upon the cessation of conceptual constructions such as "existence" and so forth, he attains the signless yoga that is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

And so it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*: “Being thus skilled in [identifying] defects, he applies himself to the yoga of the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) for the sake of departing from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Abounding in the cultivation of emptiness, in whatever places his mind extends or finds delight, he thoroughly investigates those very places and penetrates them as empty. [That which is the mind, upon examining it, he also penetrates as empty. Even that mind by which he examines, when thoroughly investigated in terms of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [is likewise found to be empty].”
He penetrates emptiness;
examining it in this way, he enters into yoga with signlessness.
By this, exactly that is demonstrated.
But for one who does not investigate, there is no entry into signlessness.
Thus, as he investigates the intrinsic nature of phenomena and does not perceive it, he then does not conceptualize that "it exists," nor does he conceptualize that "it does not exist."
Because that which is conceptualized as "non-existent" never appears at all in the mind;
for if an entity had ever been seen, one might then conceptualize its non-existence through its negation.
When, even upon investigating with wisdom throughout the three times, the yogi does not perceive any entity, then of what could he conceive "it does not exist" by way of negation?
Thus, at that time, no other conceptual constructions exist for him,
because all conceptual construction is pervaded by the two conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.
Thus, due to the absence of the pervader, there is also the absence of the pervaded.
This being so, one enters into the state of non-proliferation and non-conceptuality, and becomes non-reliant upon form and the other sense objects.
And by investigating with wisdom, because one does not perceive the intrinsic nature of any entity whatsoever, one becomes a meditator for whom wisdom is supreme.
Having thus entered into reality consisting of the selflessness of persons and phenomena,
there is no further object remaining to be examined.
With a mind in which discursive thought has ceased, which is of a single non-conceptual flavor and flows by its own natural force,
the yogi should remain, without deliberate effort, clearly discerning that very reality.
And remaining therein, he should not allow the binding of the mind to be distracted.
When one perceives that the mind has become distracted outwardly in the interim, then, having stilled that distraction by means of examining its own nature,
one should again direct the mind toward that very same object with increasing intensity.
However, when one perceives that the mind is no longer finding delight therein, [one should apply the appropriate remedy].
Then, by seeing the virtues of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one should cultivate delight in it;
and by seeing the faults in distraction, one should pacify any lack of delight.
Furthermore, when one perceives that the mind has become sluggish due to its activity being overcome by sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*), [one should apply the appropriate remedy].
Or, if there is a suspicion of laxity, the practitioner should pacify that laxity by attending to an object of joy, such as the form of the Buddha, or by attending to the perception of light;
thereafter, he should grasp that very reality more firmly.
However, when the yogi does not perceive reality with great clarity—like one born blind, or like a person who has entered darkness, or like one with eyes closed—[he must apply the remedies].
Then his mind should be understood as sunken and devoid of insight (vipaśyanā).
Or, if he should observe that in the interim the mind has become excited through longing for objects previously experienced, or if it is suspected of being agitated;
Then, one should pacify restlessness by reflecting on objects that inspire a sense of urgency, such as impermanence.
Thereafter, one should again exert effort toward the effortless flow of the mind upon that very reality.
And when the mind becomes unstable in its movement, like a distracted man or a monkey, [one should apply the appropriate remedy].
That should be understood as restlessness, and it is also characterized by the absence of calm abiding (*śamatha*).

Then, when the mind arises toward that very reality—having become free from both laxity and restlessness, proceeding in equilibrium, flowing spontaneously, and becoming even more vivid—one should practice equanimity by relaxing the effort of mental application (*ābhoga*).
At that time, it should be known that the path which carries the union of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā-yuganaddha*) has been accomplished.

And when one cultivates insight (*vipaśyanā*), if one cultivates it with an excess of wisdom (*prajñā*), then because calm abiding (*śamatha*) is deficient, the mind will waver like a lamp placed in a windy spot; consequently, the vision of reality will not be very clear.
Therefore, at that time, calm abiding must be cultivated.
If there is an excess of calm abiding (*śamatha*), the vision of reality will not be very clear, like that of a person overcome by drowsiness;
therefore, at that time, wisdom (*prajñā*) should be cultivated.

When both [calm abiding and insight] proceed in equilibrium, like a pair of oxen yoked together pulling a load, then one should remain without further effort as long as no affliction of body or mind arises.
In brief, there are six faults of every meditative concentration:
laziness, loss of the object of focus, mental sinking, and so forth.
Excitement, lack of application, and application.
As their antidotes, eight formative forces of abandonment (prahāṇasaṃskāra) are to be cultivated:
faith (śraddhā), aspiration (chanda),
and exertion (vyāyāma).
serenity,
mindfulness, and clear comprehension;
These are volition and equanimity.
Among them, the first four are the antidotes to laziness.
For instance: through faith, characterized by deep conviction in the qualities of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the practitioner's aspiration arises.
From that, the one possessing aspiration initiates vigor (*vīrya*).
Then, from the initiation of vigor, he cultivates the pliancy (*karmanyatā*) of body and mind.
Then, for one whose body and mind are pliant, laziness is turned away.
Therefore, faith and the other [faculties] serve to abandon laziness; for that purpose, they should be cultivated.
Mindfulness is the antidote to the loss of the object of focus;
clear comprehension is the antidote to lethargy and excitement,
because by means of it, one abandons those two while maintaining equanimity.
However, at the time when laxity and excitement have not been pacified, there is the fault of non-application; therefore, as their antidote, volition should be cultivated.
Once laxity and excitement have been pacified, if the mind should become diverted from that state of tranquility, [one must apply effort].
That is the fault of over-exertion (*ābhoga*).
Its antidote is that at that time one should cultivate equanimity (*upekṣā*);
if over-exertion is applied when the mind has attained evenness, [it becomes a fault].
At that time, the mind becomes distracted;
even when the mind is sluggish, if no mental application is exerted,
then, due to being devoid of insight (vipaśyanā), [the mind remains in that state].
The mind would become sluggish like a blind man;
therefore, one should restrain the sluggish mind and pacify the agitated mind.
Once again, he should remain in equanimity upon attaining meditative absorption.
Then, for as long as he desires, the yogi should remain cultivating reality precisely without any further volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

However, when pain arises in the body or elsewhere, he should repeatedly, in the interim, survey the entire world and descend into the realization that it appears like an illusion, a mirage, the moon reflected in water, or a reflection.
And so it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśa*: "One perceives all phenomena as equal to the expanse of space by means of supramundane gnosis;
furthermore, by means of the subsequently attained [gnosis], one perceives them as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, or the moon reflected in water.
Thus, having understood the world to be like an illusion,
Having brought forth great compassion toward sentient beings, one should reflect as follows:

"These people of immature intellect, not understanding such profundity of the Dharma, are inverted by their superimposition of existence and other qualities onto phenomena that are primordially peaceful; consequently, they accumulate various karmas and afflictions and thus wander in saṃsāra."
Then I shall act in such a way that I may cause them to realize this kind of profundity of the Dharma;
then, having rested, he should again enter the samādhi of the non-appearance of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanirābhāsa*) in the same manner.
When there is weariness of mind, [he should rest].
In that same manner, having rested, one should descend again.
Thus, by this sequence, one should remain for as long as one is able—whether for a *ghaṭikā*, [or half a watch], or for one full watch.
Then, desiring to rise from meditative absorption, one should reflect thus even without breaking the cross-legged posture:

"Even though all these phenomena are indeed unarisen from the perspective of ultimate reality, nevertheless, like an illusion, they appear as various and distinct through the power of a specific collection of causes and conditions; thus, they are delightful so long as they are not analyzed.
Therefore, there is no consequence of falling into the view of nihilism."

Nor does it fall into the extreme of denial, because when analyzed with wisdom they are not apprehended; therefore, there is no consequence of the view of eternalism, nor of the extreme of superimposition.

In this regard, those who, being deprived of the eye of wisdom and possessing perverted minds, are attached to a self and perform various karmas, they wander about in *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, those who are exclusively turned away from *saṃsāra* and, due to a lack of great compassion, do not fulfill the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as giving for the sake of sentient beings, yet discipline themselves— they fall into the enlightenment of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* because of their lack of skillful means (*upāya*).

But those who, having realized that the world is without intrinsic nature, resolve to uplift the entire world through the power of great compassion, and— like magicians— their intellects being free from error, they fully accumulate the vast equipment of merit and knowledge; having attained the state of a Tathāgata, they remain until the end of saṃsāra, accomplishing the welfare and happiness of the entire world in every possible way.

And by the power of the accumulation of wisdom (*jñāna-sambhāra*), they do not fall into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) because they have abandoned all afflictions (*kleśa*); and by virtue of the vast and immeasurable accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*) they have gathered out of regard for all sentient beings, they become the source of sustenance for all sentient beings.

Therefore, one who desires to establish the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings and wishes to attain non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) must always apply oneself to the acquisition of the vast accumulations of merit and wisdom.
And so it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*: "The accumulation of wisdom leads to the abandonment of all afflictions;
the accumulation of merit leads to being the sustenance for all sentient beings.
Therefore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should always apply himself to both the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wisdom."
And it is said in the *Āryatathāgatotpattisambhavasūtra*: "Furthermore, this manifestation of the Tathāgatas does not arise from a single cause.
For what reason? [Because...]"
"O sons of the Conqueror, Tathāgatas arise through ten kinds of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of causes brought together.
What are these ten? Namely, by way of the cause of the insatiable attainment of the immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom," and so forth.

And it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "The bodies of the Tathāgata are born from a hundredfold merit; they are born from all wholesome dharmas; they are born from the karma of immeasurable roots of virtue," and so forth.

Having done thus, slowly breaking the cross-legged posture and prostrating to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the ten directions, and having offered them worship, hymns of praise, and gifts, one should make the vow of the Noble Bhadracaryā and so forth. Thereafter, one should be intent upon acquiring the entire accumulation of merit consisting of generosity and the rest, dedicated toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and permeated by emptiness and compassion.
But as for one who thinks:
"Sentient beings wander in saṃsāra, experiencing the fruits of their karma such as rebirth in heaven, by the power of virtuous and non-virtuous actions produced from mental conceptualization;
however, those who do not think of anything at all and do not perform any action whatsoever are completely liberated from saṃsāra."
Therefore, nothing at all should be contemplated,
nor should any virtuous practice such as giving be performed;
it is only with reference to foolish people that the virtuous practices of giving and so forth have been taught.
By that, the entirety of the Mahāyāna would be rejected.
Since all vehicles have the Mahāyāna as their root, by rejecting it, every vehicle whatsoever would be rejected.
For instance, for one who says "nothing at all should be contemplated," wisdom characterized by the correct analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) would be rejected.
Since right knowledge has its root in the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), by rejecting that [discernment], supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-prajñā*) would also be rejected.
By rejecting that, omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) would be rejected.
Furthermore, by one who says that the practice of generosity and so forth need not be performed, the means (*upāya*) consisting of generosity and the rest is most clearly rejected.
The Mahāyāna is summarized as precisely this: namely, wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).
As it is said in the *Āryagayāśīrṣa*: "These two are the concise paths of the bodhisattvas.
Which two? Namely—" (Bhk 233)
Wisdom and skillful means are also mentioned in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*, which states: "These two—wisdom and skillful means—contribute to the inclusion of all the perfections for bodhisattvas.
Consequently, one who rejects the Mahāyāna would commit a great karmic obstruction.
Therefore, [it is for one who rejects the Mahāyāna,
who has heard little,
and who clings to the view of a self...]
Since he has not served learned men, has not ascertained the principles of the Tathāgata’s teaching, is himself ruined, and ruins others as well— being corrupted by both logic and scripture—

his speech, being mixed with poison like poisoned food, must be avoided from afar by any wise person who desires their own welfare. For, by rejecting the correct analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), he would be rejecting the very primary factor of enlightenment known as the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

And without the analytical examination of the elements (*dharmapravicaya*), how could the mind of a yogin— who has been habituated since beginningless time to the clinging to the existence of form and so forth— enter into a state free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatā*)?
If it is argued that he enters by means of non-recollection and non-mental engagement (*asmṛtyamanasikāra*) toward all phenomena, that is incorrect.

For indeed, without the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), it is impossible to achieve non-recollection (*asmṛti*) or non-attention (*amanasikāra*) even toward all phenomena that are being experienced.

Moreover, if one were to cultivate non-recollection and non-attention toward those phenomena by cultivating the thought, "These phenomena must not be recollected by me, nor should they be attended to," then, on the contrary, they would become even more thoroughly recollected and attended to by him.

Now, if "non-recollection" and "non-mental engagement" are intended merely as the absence of recollection and mental engagement, then it is precisely this that must be investigated: by what means does their absence come about?
Furthermore, it is not logical for a non-entity to be a cause.
By means of which [the non-conceptual state] might arise from that signless non-attention—

if non-conceptuality were to result from that alone— then it would follow that even one who is in a state of swoon would enter into non-conceptuality, due to the absence of mindfulness and attention. Furthermore, apart from the analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), there is no other means by which one could effect such non-recollection and non-attention.

Moreover, even if non-recollection and non-mental attention were possible, how could the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of phenomena be understood without the analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*)?
For phenomena do not [lack intrinsic nature] by their very own nature.
If one were to think "they abide as empty" without that very investigation, there would be no penetration of their emptiness;
nor is the abandonment of obscurations possible without the penetration of emptiness, because otherwise it would follow that everyone everywhere would be liberated.
Furthermore, if for that yogin mindfulness and mental attention do not operate toward all phenomena—whether due to a lapse of mindfulness or through delusion—[then there can be no realization].
In that case, how could such an utterly deluded person be a yogi?
Without the analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), the cultivation of non-recollection and non-mental engagement therein would result only in the cultivation of delusion itself;
consequently, the light of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) would be cast far away.
Now, if he is neither one whose mindfulness is lost nor one who is deluded,

then how could he possibly effect non-recollection and non-mental attention therein without the analytical investigation of reality? For it is not the case that one who is actually remembering fails to remember.
It is not logical to say that one sees while yet not seeing;
furthermore, how could the arising of the Buddha-qualities such as the recollection of former existences occur through the practice of non-recollection and non-attention, given their contradiction?
For indeed, for one who is practicing cold which is opposed to heat, there would be no experience of the sensation of heat.
Furthermore, if a yogin who has entered meditative absorption possesses mental consciousness, then it must necessarily have some object of perception.
For it is not possible for ordinary beings to suddenly possess a cognition that is without an object.
If such [cognition] does not exist, then how could the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of phenomena be understood?
And by what antidote would the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) be abandoned?
Furthermore, the cessation of the mind is not possible for an ordinary person who has not attained the fourth dhyāna.

Therefore, those two—non-recollection (*asmṛti*) and non-attention (*amanasikāra*)—which are recited in the True Dharma, should be understood as being preceded by the correct analytical observation (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*).
Through this correct analytical observation, non-recollection and non-attention can be achieved, and not otherwise.
For instance, when a yogi, investigating with correct wisdom, does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever as having arisen ultimately throughout the three times,
how then could he apply mindfulness and mental attention toward it? For how could that which is ultimately unexperienced because of its non-existence even in the three times be remembered?
Or, it may be brought to mind;
then he would enter that non-conceptual knowledge in which all conceptual proliferation has ceased.
By entering that, he penetrates emptiness, and by that penetration, he becomes one who has abandoned the entire web of false views.
Being endowed with skillful means and through the cultivation of wisdom, one becomes proficient in both the conventional and ultimate truths;
therefore, by attaining unobstructed knowledge, one realizes all the qualities of a Buddha.
Therefore, without the analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), there is neither the arising of right knowledge nor the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Thus it is said in the *Mañjuśrīvikurvaṇasūtra*: "How, daughter, does a bodhisattva become one who has conquered the battle?
She replied: "O Mañjuśrī, he who, having investigated and investigated all phenomena, does not perceive them."
Therefore, having conquered the enemies that are the afflictions with the weapon of wisdom by means of the wide-open eye of knowledge,
the yogi dwells fearlessly,
and not like a cowardly man with eyes closed.

It is also said in the *Āryasamādhirāja*: "If one examines the phenomena of selflessness, and having examined them, meditates upon them, that is the cause for attaining the fruit of nirvāṇa; any other cause does not lead to peace."
And it is said in the *Sūtrasamuccaya*: “To dwell engaged in the yoga of insight (*vipaśyanā*) oneself, yet not to encourage others toward insight, is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, insight has the nature of the discernment of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), as stated in the *Āryaratnamegha*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and other texts.
And in the *Āryaratnamegha*: “For one who examines insight, the entry into the signless (*animitta*) is said to result from the penetration of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).”
And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: “Because,
Mahāmati,
when things are investigated by means of the intellect, their specific and general characteristics are not apprehended.”
"Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature.
In various sūtras, the Blessed One has taught manifold forms of analytical investigation; these would be contradicted if true analytical investigation were not to be performed.
Therefore, it is appropriate to say: "We are of little wisdom and little vigor; we are unable to seek out extensive learning.
For it is not right to reject that, since the Blessed One has praised extensive learning in many ways.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*: "Those who are disconnected from reflection regarding inconceivable phenomena—for them, it is improper (ayoniśas).

In that context, those who conceptually construct the arising of phenomena that are ultimately unarisen, and who engage in reflection like the Śrāvakas and others by way of impermanence, suffering, and so forth—they initiate reflection through the extremes of superimposition and denial; for them, that becomes improper. The statement made there to negate that [reflection] is not a negation of authentic analytical inspection (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*), because that [authentic inspection] is...
Because it is authorized in all the sūtras;

and likewise, it is said in that very same *Brahmaparipṛcchā*: "The Bodhisattva who is a hero of mind said: 'He who contemplates all phenomena with the mind, yet remains therein unhurt and unimpaired—he is therefore called a Bodhisattva.'"
In that very same place it is said: "How do they become possessed of vigor?
When, while searching for the mind of omniscience, they do not perceive it.
Again, in that very same place it is said: "And they will be wise by means of their thorough investigation of phenomena."

And: "The Dharma is not realized by means of hearing and reflection; it is realized only through meditative cultivation. And: "The Dharma
It should be understood that by negating their conceit, the fact that phenomena are to be personally realized is established; thus,
the negation is made regarding improper mental engagement (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), not regarding authentic analytical investigation (*bhūta-pratyavekṣā*).
Otherwise, there would be much more that contradicts both reason and scripture,
as was stated previously.
Furthermore, only that which has been understood through the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection is to be cultivated by the wisdom consisting of meditation, and nothing else.
It is like a horse running on a track that has been pointed out.
Therefore, one must perform the analytical investigation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*).

Even though this [investigation] is by nature conceptual, because it is by nature appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*), non-conceptual knowledge of reality arises from it; thus, one who seeks that knowledge should cultivate it.
And when the fire of the knowledge of reality, which is free from conceptual construction,
has arisen,
being present,
It is stated in the *Āryaratnakūṭa* that just as two pieces of wood are consumed by the fire produced from their friction, so too is that [wisdom] later consumed by that very same [fire].

Furthermore, regarding the claim that "no action, whether wholesome or otherwise, need be performed," if one were to speak in that way, it would amount to accepting the doctrine of the Ājīvikas, who maintain that liberation results from the exhaustion of karma.
For in the teaching of the Blessed One, liberation is not held to result from the exhaustion of karma;
rather, it results from the exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Indeed, it is impossible to bring about the exhaustion of karma accumulated since beginningless time, because it is infinite.

Furthermore, because while one is experiencing the fruit of that [karma] in the miserable realms and so forth, other karma continues to be produced; and because as long as the afflictions remain unimpaired, they stand as the cause for that [production], making it impossible to stop karma—
just as a lamp’s light cannot be stopped when the lamp itself is not extinguished—
and because, as was stated previously, the destruction of the afflictions is not possible for one who denies the practice of insight (vipaśyanā).

If it is thought that insight (vipaśyanā) must be cultivated for the sake of the destruction of afflictions (kleśa), then since liberation is accomplished through the destruction of afflictions alone, effort toward the destruction of karma would be useless. It is indeed correct that unwholesome karma should not be performed; however, [the argument fails here].
But why is the wholesome (kuśala) prohibited? If it is argued that it is prohibited because it brings about cyclic existence (saṃsāra), that is incorrect.

Only that wholesome action which is produced by the perversions regarding the self and so forth leads to cyclic existence; however, this is not the case for the wholesome actions of Bodhisattvas, which are produced by great compassion and dedicated toward unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Likewise, in the *Āryadaśabhūmika*, it is stated that these very same ten paths of wholesome action become the vehicles for the states of Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha through the specific purity of dedication and other such factors.
It is taught in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*:

"Just as the mass of water from all great rivers that have entered the great ocean [becomes one], so too the roots of virtue accumulated by Bodhisattvas through various means, when dedicated toward omniscience, become of a single flavor with omniscience."
Thus it has been described. Furthermore,

the purity of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the field (*kṣetra*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as their excellence consisting of radiance, retinue, great enjoyments, and so forth, exist because they are the fruit of the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) such as generosity, as stated in various sūtras.
That which was described by the Blessed One would also be contradicted;
furthermore, if virtuous conduct were prohibited, the Prātimokṣa vows and so forth would also be rejected.
Consequently, it would follow that his shaving of the head, wearing of the saffron robes, and other such acts would be entirely in vain.

Furthermore, when there is aversion toward the performance of wholesome karma, one will have cultivated aversion toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and aversion toward acting for the benefit of sentient beings;
consequently, awakening (*bodhi*) would be far from him.

For it is said in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*: "I have not declared that unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening belongs to one who is exclusively averse to the welfare of sentient beings and exclusively averse to the performance of conditioned formations."
And in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā* and other texts, it is described: "Aversion toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is the ultimate immorality for bodhisattvas;
whereas the embracing of cyclic existence is the supreme morality.
And it is said in the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa*: "For bodhisattvas, entering cyclic existence through skillful means (*upāya*) constitutes liberation."
Wisdom devoid of skillful means is bondage; skillful means devoid of wisdom is bondage.
Skillful means accompanied by wisdom is liberation.
It is described that "wisdom conjoined with skillful means is liberation.
In the *Āryagaganagañja*, it is said: "Weariness with saṃsāra is a deed of Māra for bodhisattvas.
And in the *Sūtrasamuccaya*: "To contemplate the unconditioned while becoming weary of conditioned wholesome deeds is a deed of Māra."
"To understand the path to enlightenment but not to seek the path of the perfections (pāramitā) is the work of Māra.
Furthermore, it is said in that same [text]: "From attachment to the mind of giving up to attachment to the mind of wisdom is the work of Māra.

In this context, there is no prohibition against practicing giving and the other perfections; rather, [the fault lies] in one who is attached to a mind of "I" and "mine," or attached to a mind of subject and object.
This is the negation of that perverse adherence to generosity and so forth which belongs to one who perceives [phenomena] as real entities.
For it is said that generosity and the like are "works of Māra" because they are impure when produced by perverse adherence;
otherwise, even meditative concentration would not be something to be practiced.
And in that case, how could liberation occur?

(Bhk 239) For this very reason, in order to demonstrate that for one who perceives [objects], the practice of giving and so forth is impure due to the notion of a plurality of sentient beings, it is said in the *Āryagaganagañja*: "For one who possesses the notion of a plurality of sentient beings [and of perverted karma]..."
It has been stated that giving and the other perfections are the work of Māra.

Furthermore, regarding the dedication of the three aggregates, it was said: "One who does not understand the equality of all giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom perceives them through apprehension;
thus, by means of that gift sought after, and by that morality grasped at, one maintains morality."

“‘I confess that [the thought] “patience has been cultivated by one who perceives self and other,” and so forth’— even in that case, it is merely established that for one who perceives [objects] and possesses the notion of diversity, even acts such as giving, when arising from a perverted adherence, do not become pure. However, this is not a total prohibition against practicing giving and the other perfections.”
Otherwise, confession would have been prescribed for all acts such as giving without distinction, rather than only for one who has fallen into the error of apprehension (*upalambha-viparyāsa*).
Furthermore, it is said in the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*: "Whatever conduct there may be, it is all a mental construction."
"Enlightenment is also beyond conceptualization," and so forth.
In that context as well, because the practice involving conceptualizations such as arising and so on is the subject at hand, its nature as conceptualization has been stated.
Furthermore, the prophecy is granted to a bodhisattva who abides in the signless dwelling and proceeds without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Only this much has been established— that [the perfection of giving] belongs to no other;
furthermore, it has been elucidated that all practices, such as giving and the rest, are ultimately unarisen,
but it has not been stated that the practice itself should not be performed.

Otherwise, in the *Dīpaṅkara-avadāna*, regarding those Buddhas whom the Blessed One served, whose names could not be fully recounted by the Blessed One even if he were to speak for an entire eon— how is it that the Blessed One did not prohibit their conduct while they were in the state of a bodhisattva?
At that time, Dīpaṅkara did not indeed prohibit the Blessed One's conduct;
rather, when he was seen established on the eighth stage in the peaceful dwelling of the signless, he was then prophesied by the Blessed One, and therein his conduct [was affirmed]. (Bhk 240)
It is not prohibited;

however, that supreme state of dwelling in the signless (*animittavihāraparamatā*) of the bodhisattvas is prohibited by the Buddhas of the ten stages at the eighth stage, thinking, "Let this not be their final nirvāṇa. This is provided, however, that the practice is not to be abandoned in every respect.
If that were the case, everything previously stated would be contradicted;

and furthermore, it has been said in that very *Brahmaparipṛcchā*: “One gives a gift and does not long for its maturation; one guards morality and does not superimpose [grasping] upon it,” and so forth.

"Bodhisattvas endowed with four Brahma-qualities become irreversible from the Buddha-dharmas. By which four? [They are: embracing an immeasurable saṃsāra, serving and making offerings to immeasurable Buddhas," and so forth; otherwise, all of this would be contradicted.
Nor is it reasonable to say that the practice must be performed only by one of dull faculties and not by one of sharp faculties;
for from the first stage up to those bodhisattvas established in the tenth stage, the practice of giving and so forth arises,
and because of the statement that one does not fail to carry them out in the remaining stages.
For even those who have entered the stages are not necessarily endowed with dull faculties.

In the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*, it is described: "Only by one established in the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) should the giving, great giving, and supreme giving be performed.
And in the *Sūtrasamuccaya*, it is described: "A bodhisattva who possesses the practice of the six perfections and so forth attains the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgatas."
There is no movement swifter than the movement of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).

Nor is there any other path for Bodhisattvas apart from the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) that could carry them more swiftly. Furthermore, it is described in the Sūtras [and stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*, the *Daśabhūmika*, and so forth] that the purification of the mental continuum occurs only gradually, like the purification of gold: "When one is established in suchness (*tathatā*)..."
At that time, one has entered the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Thereafter, by gradually purifying the preceding stages, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, there is no other gateway for entering the city of Buddhahood simultaneously apart from the stages and the perfections (*pāramitā*), nor has any such thing been taught by the Blessed One anywhere in the sūtras or elsewhere.

If it is argued that because the six perfections are included within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) itself, by practicing that alone all the perfections are practiced, and therefore the other perfections such as giving (*dāna*) need not be practiced separately— then, by that same logic,
since the six perfections are included even in a Buddha’s cow-dung mandala, one would have to perform only the mandala and not the meditative concentrations and so forth.

Even for a Śrāvaka who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*), because [the afflictions] do not manifest due to the very absence of signs (*nimitta*), there would follow the consequence that he has fulfilled the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) at that time.
Consequently, no distinction between Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas would be established.

However, in order to demonstrate that the six perfections must be fulfilled by a Bodhisattva in every state whatsoever, the Blessed One showed that all the perfections are included within each individual perfection.
Furthermore, it is not that only a single perfection is to be practiced.

Thus it is said in the *Sarvadharmavaipulya*: "Maitreya, regarding this attainment of the six perfections for the sake of the complete enlightenment of bodhisattvas, those deluded persons will speak thus:"
"A Bodhisattva should train in the perfection of wisdom alone; what is the use of the remaining perfections?"—
they will think that those other perfections are to be disparaged.
What do you think, Ajita? Was that King of Kāśī lacking in wisdom, who gave his own flesh to the hawk for the sake of the dove?
Maitreya said, "Certainly not, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said, "Maitreya, those roots of merit associated with the six perfections which were accumulated by me while practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva— "
"Have those roots of merit been diminished?
Maitreya replied,
"Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Ajita, you yourself have for sixty kalpas accomplished the perfection of giving;
likewise, you have for sixty kalpas accomplished everything up to the perfection of wisdom."
"Regarding that, those deluded persons will say:

'Awakening is by means of a single method alone, namely, the method of emptiness'; yet they fail to purify their conduct. And so forth; by practicing emptiness alone, they fall into nirvana like the śrāvakas.
Therefore, wisdom conjoined with skillful means must be cultivated.
For this very reason, the venerable master Nāgārjuna stated in the *Sūtrasamuccaya*: "A bodhisattva who lacks skill in means should not apply himself to the profound nature of phenomena.
In this regard, he has cited the *Āryavimalakīrtinirdeśa* and other such sources as evidence.

Furthermore, it is improper for a discerning person to abandon the words of the venerable master Nāgārjuna—which are endowed with both logic and scripture—and the words of the Blessed One, in order to accept the words of some other foolish person.

And in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*, it is stated: "Emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects should be cultivated by virtue of being possessed of all the virtues such as generosity; it is not [to be cultivated] alone."

And it is said in the *Āryaratnakūṭa*: “Kāśyapa, just as kings, when supported by their ministers, accomplish all their tasks, even so the wisdom of a bodhisattva, when supported by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), accomplishes all the works of a Buddha. For this very reason, let there be no entry into nirvāṇa for one who practices emptiness alone.”
It is also stated by the Blessed One in the *Āryatathāgataguhyasūtra*: "One should not practice 'mind-only' exclusively without an object;
rather, it was said for the purpose of demonstrating that skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) must also be practiced. For example, noble son, fire burns because of fuel."
Without grasping, it is stilled;
in the same way, the mind burns because of an object,
and without an object, it is stilled.
Therein, the bodhisattva skilled in means understands both the pacification of the focal object purified by the perfection of wisdom,
yet he does not cause the focal object of the roots of virtue to cease,
nor does he give rise to the focal object of the afflictions.
He arouses the objective support of the perfections,
he contemplates the objective support of emptiness, and he regards the objective support of great compassion for all sentient beings. For in this way, noble son,
a bodhisattva who is skillful in means and purified by the perfection of wisdom attains mastery over the absence of objective supports.
Having spoken thus in detail, he further says as follows: "There is no object whatsoever that does not serve to bring about the wisdom of omniscience for a bodhisattva;
for that bodhisattva, all objects have been dedicated toward awakening."
This bodhisattva, skilled in means, perceives all phenomena as conforming to awakening.
For example, noble son,
there is nothing in this trichiliocosm that would not be for the enjoyment of sentient beings.
"In the same way, noble son, there is no object whatsoever that a bodhisattva skilled in means does not see as being conducive to awakening"—thus it is said at length.
In this manner, the practice of wisdom and skillful means for bodhisattvas is taught in infinite sūtras.

In that regard, even if one is unable to personally initiate the vigor of the accumulation of merit through giving and so forth, it is nevertheless not proper to give such instruction to others; thus, one would commit an injury to both oneself and others.

Thus, it has been established through both reasoning and scripture that a bodhisattva must necessarily engage in the contemplation of reality (*bhūtapratyavekṣā*) and accumulate the entire equipment of merit consisting of generosity and the other perfections.

Therefore, a discerning person, having cast aside like poison the words of those of little learning who are full of conceit, and following the nectar-like words of wise men such as the noble Nāgārjuna and others,

should generate great compassion for all sentient beings and, remaining free from error like a magician, apply themselves to the practice of all virtuous deeds— generosity and the rest— which are dedicated toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
And one should cultivate the resolve to be intent upon the deliverance of the entire world without exception,
as it is said in the *Āryadharmasaṃgīti*:
"Just as a certain magician would strive to liberate a magical creation,"
And he has no attachment to that emanation, since it was previously known by him to be such.

Having realized that the three realms of existence are like a magical illusion, those who have reached the further shore of perfect enlightenment don their armor for the sake of the world, even though they already know the world as it truly is.
Thus,
for one who constantly and respectfully practices both wisdom and skillful means, through the gradual ripening of the mental continuum and the arising of ever-purer moments,
by reaching the ultimate limit of the cultivation of the true object, there occurs a clear realization of the *dharmadhātu* that is free from the entire web of conceptual construction.
Immaculate supramundane knowledge arises, like a steady lamp in a windless place;
at that time, the objective support consisting of the limit of phenomena is attained,
and one has entered the path of seeing.
The first stage is attained;

then, by purifying the stages that follow it in succession, and upon the removal of all obscurations like gold, one attains unattached and unimpeded gnosis and reaches the stage of a Buddha, the foundation of all qualities without exception.
And one obtains the objective support that is the perfection of the task;
therefore, one who desires to attain Buddhahood should apply oneself, for the time being, to the Middle Way.
Whatever merit has been attained by me through elucidating this incomparable path,
may all beings, by that merit, attain the middle path.
For the virtuous, having cast away the impurities of envy and the like, are never satiated by qualities, just as the ocean is never sated by waters;
having discerned them, they accept well-spoken words, just as swans joyfully extract milk from water.
Therefore, the wise have removed from their minds that which is clouded by partiality;
every well-spoken word, even from a child, should be accepted.
The *Bhāvanākrama* composed by Ācārya Kamalaśīla at the end is completed.
The third *Bhāvanākrama* is completed.
